Malacañang on Friday called on groups planning to hold rallies on September 21 to keep their demonstrations peaceful and avoid violence.
Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the government is preparing for possible developments during the protests marking the anniversary of the declaration of martial law.

“Hindi po ito hinahadlangan ng Pangulo ang kanilang pag-ga-gather, ang kanilang freedom of expression ay hindi po ito hahadlangan kailanman ng Pangulo,” Castro said in an interview on GMA News’ Unang Balita.
(The President is not preventing them from gathering. Their freedom of expression will never be prevented by the President.)

“Ang nais lang po sana natin, ang ating dasal ay huwag maging marahas. At kung may mga nangyari noong nakaraang taon, sana hindi po mangyari at hindi naman po sila hinahadlangan ng pamahalaan sa kanilang mga gagawing protesta,” she added.

(We just hope for, our prayer is that there will be no violence. And if there were things that happened last year, I hope they will not happen again but the government is not preventing them from protesting.)
The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) and the Philippine National Police (PNP) are also preparing for the protests, Castro said.
The September 21 rallies will be held to commemorate the declaration of Martial Law in 1972.
Castro said authorities would observe maximum tolerance toward protesters while carrying out their duties during the demonstrations. —Joviland Rita/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
articles.summary: The White House removed Larsson's Midnight Sun from one of its reels after the artist called the clip "dehumanising".

blocks.text: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.

The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.
The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".

In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.
Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.
In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".
Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people."
"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".

"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.
Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.
White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.

Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".

Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

articles.title: Marcos has no plans to resign, Palace says
articles.summary: Marcos has no plans to resign, Palace says

blocks.text: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has no plans to resign from office, Malacañang said on Friday following remarks from Vice President Sara Duterte’s camp that she is prepared to take over.
“Unang-una, walang magre-resign,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro told GMA News’ Unang Balita in an interview.
(First of all, no one will resign.)
“Wish lang nila 'yun dahil ang Pangulo tumutupad sa kanyang tungkulin at nagtatrabaho para sa bayan, sa bansa, at sa taumbayan. So kung wish nila na magre-resign ang Pangulo, I'm sorry,” she added.
(They just wish because the President is fulfilling his duties and working for the country and the people. So if they wish that the President would resign, I'm sorry.)

Castro also responded to claims from Duterte’s camp that senators, police officials, and other government personalities are being controlled by Malacañang in connection with the Vice President’s impeachment case.

She said government agencies are simply carrying out their respective mandates and that Duterte should address the issues and complaints raised against her rather than accuse the government of persecution.

Castro criticized Duterte’s camp for questioning the administration while, according to Castro, they are failing to explain issues in her impeachment case including the use of confidential funds, as well as the grave threat case involving an alleged plot to kill Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Zaldy Co, Roque, Legarda
Meanwhile, Castro was also asked about possible legal actions or operations involving former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque, ex-lawmaker Zaldy Co, and Senator Loren Legarda.
She declined to provide details on any operations.
“Hindi ko na po ito mai-re-reveal on air,” Castro said.
(I can’t re-reveal it on air.)

“Sa ngayon hindi ko masasabi kung ano yung mga legal na operasyon nila. Sabi nga natin ay hindi natin puwede maisiwalat kung ano-ano ang dapat na gawin, mga legal na operasyon, at baka hindi matupad o hindi maisagawa dahil nalaman na po noong dapat na makuha, mahuli, mapadala sa Pilipinas. So, hayaan na lang po natin si Secretary Jonvic dyan,” she added.

(Right now I can’t say what their legal operations are. As I have said, we can’t reveal what needs to be done, the legal operations, and it might not be done or not be carried out because it was already revealed when they were supposed to be captured, caught, or sent to the Philippines. So, let’s just leave it to Secretary Jonvic.)
In May 2025, warrants of arrest were issued against Roque, Cassandra Ong, and 48 others for qualified human trafficking in relation with the alleged scam hub run by Lucky South 99.

He has denied his role in the operations but has acknowledged providing legal counsel to Whirlwind Corporation, the owner of the land on which stood a raided POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga where criminal activities such as torture and scams apparently took place.
Roque has sought asylum from the Netherlands but his case has been referred to Austrian authorities since they were the ones to issue him a visa.
Arrest warrants were issued against Co and 17 others over supposed anomalous flood control projects in November 2025.

The Ombudsman filed with the Sandiganbayan corruption and malversation of public funds charges against Co and others. These charges were in connection with the alleged anomalous P289-million flood control project in Oriental Mindoro.
Co has denied the allegations.

In August this year, the Office of the Ombudsman ordered Legarda and her son Batangas First District Representative Leandro Leviste to answer the plunder and graft complaints against them over the alleged failure of Leviste’s firm to provide solar power as provided under its congressional franchise.
Legarda's camp called the probe “lawfare” and “political persecution.”

Legarda and Leviste left the Philippines on separate flights on August 2, according to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI). Legarda flew to France while Leviste to Hong Kong. —Joviland Rita/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: What Philippines' aging population means, and what can be done
articles.summary: Fewer Filipinos are being born. What comes next?

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 8:50am
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines' fertility rate has fallen to 1.7 children per woman, sharpening concerns that a smaller future workforce will have to support a rapidly aging population.

The Commission on Population and Development (CPD) warned that persistently low fertility could eventually weaken the country's base of workers, taxpayers and contributors to social protection systems, while increasing demand for healthcare and other services for older Filipinos.

The country's total fertility rate, or the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime based on current fertility patterns, dropped from 1.9 in 2022 to 1.7 in 2025, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.
That is well below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman.

Mylin Mirasol Quiray, information management and communications division chief of the CPD, said Thursday that the effects would become more consequential as today's smaller cohorts eventually enter the labor force.

"Low fertility rate can be a hindrance to economic progress kasi mas magiging kaunti 'yung ating mga tao na ipinapanganak na maaaring mag-earn ng money, mag-spend, mag-save," Quiray said on "Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon" radio, citing the International Monetary Fund.
(A low fertility rate can be a hindrance to economic progress because fewer people will be born who can earn money, spend and save.)
She said the more immediate concern is the country's future contributor base, as fewer births today eventually translate into fewer workers.
"'Yung declining fertility maaaring ma-weaken 'yung contributory base natin, which is fewer workers na puwedeng mapanganak," she said, citing the Philippine Institute for Development Studies.
(Declining fertility may weaken our contributory base, meaning fewer workers will be born.)
Philippines getting older
The shift is already visible in the country's age structure.
The 2024 Census of Population found that Filipinos aged 65 and older numbered 7.4 million, or 6.6% of the household population, up from 5.4% in 2020.
The country's median age also rose to 27.7 years in 2024 from 25.3 in 2020 and 24.3 in 2015, according to the PSA.
Meanwhile, Filipinos aged 60 and older reached 11.42 million, equivalent to 10.2% of the household population.
State-run research center PIDS has projected that people aged 65 and older could account for about 7.6% of the population by 2030, as the country moves further into an aging demographic structure.
Quiray said an older population would mean greater demand for public services.
"Kapag aging population na tayo, mas maraming pangangailangan 'no, sa health services, social services," she said.
(As our population ages, there will be greater demand for health services and social services.)
She said the government would need to invest earlier in health and human development so Filipinos can remain active and healthy as they age.

Recent PIDS research has warned that below-replacement fertility, combined with population aging and a potentially smaller labor force, could increase pressure on social security systems and government revenues over the longer term.
Demographic dividend still open
The demographic pressure is not immediate, however.
The Philippines still has a large working-age population. In 2024, about 74.95 million Filipinos, or 66.7% of the household population, were aged 15 to 64.
The overall dependency ratio improved to about 50 dependents for every 100 working-age Filipinos in 2024, from 57 in 2020.
Quiray said the current labor force remains large enough to support children and older dependents.
"Mas marami pa rin naman tayong workers dito sa ating population ngayon na puwedeng suportahan 'yung mga bata at saka matatanda," she said.
(We still have more workers in our population who can support children and older people.)
That gives the country time to prepare for the longer-term consequences of lower fertility.

PIDS likewise says the Philippines' demographic dividend remains open, but argues that policy must increasingly shift from controlling population growth toward building human capital and preparing for population aging.
That includes investing more heavily in early childhood development, education, healthcare and family support while the country still has a relatively large share of working-age people.
Not simply about having more children
The decline in fertility also poses a more complicated policy challenge than simply encouraging Filipinos to have bigger families.
CPD said family planning policy should continue to allow people to decide whether, when and how many children they want, rather than seek a particular fertility target.

"Kailangan pa rin natin talaga na mag-family planning para 'yung mga gustong manganak, kung kailan nila gustong manganak, ay mangyayari at kung hindi nila gustong magkaanak ay mangyayari pa rin para sa kanila," Quiray said.
(We still need family planning so that those who want to have children can do so when they choose, while those who do not want children can also make that choice.)

Modern contraceptive use among Filipino women has continued to increase, according to Quiray, rising from 41.8% in 2022 to 44.5% in 2025. Use of traditional methods such as withdrawal and the calendar method fell from 16.5% to 14.1% over the same period.
PIDS has also found that falling fertility does not necessarily mean all Filipino couples want fewer children.

Poorer households continue to have more children than they intend in some cases, while wealthier couples may have fewer children than they want, pointing to different barriers including employment insecurity, housing, caregiving responsibilities and the cost of raising a family.

articles.title: LA woman charged with murder over bus crash that preceded deadly helicopter plunge
articles.summary:
Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, accused of driving on wrong side of road to cause fatal crash NBC news helicopter was covering

A California woman was allegedly driving under the influence when she…

blocks.text: A California woman was allegedly driving under the influence when she sped down the wrong side of the road, ran a red light and plowed her SUV into a Los Angeles metro bus on Tuesday, killing two passengers, prosecutors say, in a tragedy compounded when a news helicopter covering the crash plummeted from the sky, killing three.

Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, has been charged with two counts of murder over the deaths of the two people on the bus, identified as Daniel Castillo, 46, and Gage Weida, 31. Rios was being held on $4.1m bail and is set to be arraigned on 18 September. Online court records did not list a lawyer who might speak on her behalf, and the public defender’s office did not immediately return a message about whether it was representing her.

The wake of Tuesday’s deadly bus crash took a turn for the worse in the hours after, when a local news helicopter responding to the scene crashed to the ground in a fiery ball, killing two individuals onboard: pilot George Marciniw and reporter Eliana Moreno. A pedestrian on the ground, 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, also died in the crash.

Reached Wednesday, Rios’s mother, Cindy, said she was shocked and saddened by the string of events. She said she had not spoken to her daughter since her arrest and had not been contacted by law enforcement. She could not immediately be reached on Thursday for additional comment.

Castillo left behind four children. “We are still trying to process the unimaginable reality that he is no longer with us,” his youngest daughter, Johaunna, wrote on a fundraising page for funeral expenses.
Weida’s family planned to visit him for his 32nd birthday, his father told CBS LA. “Unfortunately, we’re still heading out there, but for all the wrong reasons,” said Jeffrey Weida.
“The deadly and destructive consequences of her actions will be felt for years to come,” Los Angeles county district attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement.
Stephanie Wiggins, chief executive of the Los Angeles metro, extended her sympathies to the bus crash’s victims and their families.
“We are grateful to the first responders who rushed to the scene and to the law enforcement investigators and prosecutors working to establish the facts and pursue justice,” she said in a statement.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of the helicopter crash in Chatsworth, Los Angeles on Tuesday night. Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images

blocks.text: A vigil was planned Thursday evening to honor the victims of both crashes.

There were no immediate details on what caused the helicopter to go down, but investigators said significant clues could come from the last seconds of video the crew broadcast. In it, an alarm could be heard inside the helicopter’s cockpit as it lost altitude.
National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar said on Wednesday the video was “probably the most important evidence that we have discovered so far”.

In the video, after the beeping starts, a woman’s voice says: “Uh oh.” The helicopter moves quickly away from the bus crash site and starts losing altitude. The woman says, “You can’t pull up?” before the video stops as the chopper nears the ground.

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said the alarm suggested a potential loss of engine power and a dangerous decrease in the main rotor speed. He said the pilot appeared to be trying to perform an emergency maneuver to use the wind to force the rotor to spin again.
The NTSB is also investigating the bus collision.
Moreno and Marciniw worked for Angel City Air, a helicopter contractor, and provided aerial coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52.

Moreno, born in Orange county, joined Angel City Air in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, NBC4 said.
Marciniw grew up in southern California and graduated from Burbank high school in 1974.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the US since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.

articles.summary:
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated

At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving…

blocks.text: At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving treatment in southern Nigeria after consuming a locally brewed alcoholic concoction suspected to contain methanol, officials said on Thursday.

Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases had been reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. A total of 182 people are believed to have been affected and some are being treated in the hospital, he said.
“I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told the local TVC News channel from a hospital bed.
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated.

“This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka told The Associated Press, speaking about the drink.

Ondo state police spokesperson Abayomi Jimoh said in a statement that 15 people were arrested in connection with the incident, including one allegedly “involved in the production of substances suspected to contain methanol and is currently assisting the police with investigations.”
Locals told the AP they suspected a popular herbal drink with high alcohol content, known as “Monkey Tail,” was mixed with methanol, causing the deaths.

A trader who sells the concoction in Odigbo, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of being arrested, told the AP there are two versions of Monkey Tail: an original, safe version, and another version which is unsafe.
Local media reports said the first death was reported nearly two weeks ago.

Nigeria’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control is now enforcing a nationwide ban on alcohol in sachets and small plastic containers, which it said are easily accessible to children and young people.

articles.title: US court sentences ex-Syrian official who ran notorious ‘punishment wing’ to 60 years
articles.summary:
Samir Ousman al-Sheikh, part of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, was in charge of Adra prison where prisoners were tortured

This article contains descriptions of torture.

A US…

items: This article contains descriptions of torture.

blocks.text: A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person.

Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal jury convicted al-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms.
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence.
Al-Sheikh’s legal team and the justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Following al-Sheikh’s conviction, Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, had said in a statement that the case showed the US “is not a refuge for criminals – especially criminals who engage in the brutality of the kind this defendant inflicted on his victims”.

Al-Sheikh, 73, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 at Los Angeles international airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges.

He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the regime in just 11 days.

Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a court sentenced al-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse.
Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.

During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time.

Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet,” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die.

“[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”

Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later.
“I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani.
“Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.”

His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems.
“My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said.

Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote.

Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria.

“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court.

“This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at the Center for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”

articles.title: UN mission notes possible US war crimes in Iran strikes
articles.summary: A United Nations fact-finding mission said it found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran.

image.caption: According to Iranian authorities, more than 150 people, mainly schoolgirls, died in the strike on Minab [FILE: August 2026]Image: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Experts from the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, commissioned by the UN Human Rights Council, said they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including one that hit a school in the southern Iranian city of Minab.
In a report published Thursday, the experts also accused Iran's theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people.
Established in 2022, the mission is chaired by Bangladeshi jurist Sara Hossain and consists of independent experts.
They were expected to present their findings to the UN Human Rights Council on Monday. The Council is made up of 47 UN member countries.
The mission examined US actions during the Iran war, which started in February, and the Iranian government's response to the nationwide unrest that began in late December.
Although it is not binding, the report contributes to the international evidence gathered about the Iran war and could eventually be used in attempts to bring legal cases to international courts.
How did the US react?
The Pentagon declined to comment on the mission's report. "Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," it said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the White House issued a strongly worded statement, with spokesperson Anna Kelly saying the UN top human rights body has "accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades."

"The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Kelly said.
US strikes in Minab and Lamerd
In the report, UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe that US forces were responsible for the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab on February 28.
Iranian officials said that more than 150 people were killed in the attack, including around 120 schoolchildren.
The mission concluded that the attack was indiscriminate, causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure. This amounts to a war crime under international law, according to the report.
UN experts concluded that the school was clearly a civilian facility and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.

They reached a similar conclusion regarding a strike on a sports center in Larned, also on February 28. The report stated that the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school, killing and injuring 22 civilians.
The report concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
In a statement issued in March, US Central Command said that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd that day.
Evidence points to US role in deadly Iran school attack
Crackdown in Iran
The UN probe also found that Iranian authorities carried out widespread and systematic attacks against civilians during the protests that erupted in late December.
These attacks included unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, the report said.
According to human rights groups, bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution.
Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign adversaries, including the US and Israel.

The probe stated that it could not independently verify the death toll, but it believes that the number of deaths and injuries is likely far higher than the official count of 3,038 deaths and 25,000 injuries.

articles.title: NCR police to deploy 15,700 for Sept. 21 protests
articles.summary: More than 15,700 police personnel will be deployed ahead of Sept. 21 protests.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 7:30am

Newly appointed patrolmen and patrolwomen under the PNP's 2026 Regular and Attrition Recruitment Program assemble at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City during their oath-taking and turnover ceremonies on Sept. 16, 2026.
PNP-NCRPO / Released

MANILA, Philippines — The National Capital Region Police Office (PNP-NCRPO) will be placed on full alert status starting Saturday, September 19, in anticipation of protest actions scheduled in connection with the September 21 Martial Law commemoration.

The PNP announced that the transition to full alert status will officially begin at 12 a.m. Saturday, with full deployment of police personnel commencing at 5 p.m. that afternoon, PNP spokesperson Col. Allen Rae Co said.
More than 15,700 personnel will be deployed, according to Co.
He added that the PNP may augment its personnel with forces from Central Luzon, Calabarzon and neighboring regions if necessary.
Asked what gear police would carry, Co said personnel deployed for crowd dispersal management would have standard protective equipment, including helmets, shields and batons.
"Babalik rin po tayo sa main function ng ating kapulisan to ensure the safety of other people and 'yung infrastructures natin," Co said.
(We will also return to the main function of our police force, which is to ensure the safety of the public and our infrastructure.)
"So we have to control pag 'yung crowd natin ay naging unruly," he added. (So we have to maintain control if the crowd becomes unruly.)
The PNP, however, had yet to receive information on any rally permit applications as of Thursday morning.
He added that peaceful assemblies may be held in designated freedom parks even without a permit, subject to existing rules.

articles.title: 'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
articles.summary: Many Nigerians buy their first ever shares - in the oil refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote.

blocks.text: Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."

Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.

"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.

In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.

He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.

Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

articles.title: OpenAI asks California court to dismiss lawsuits over Tumbler Ridge shooting
articles.summary: Lawyers for OpenAI claim any legal action related to the deaths and injuries should take place in British Columbia.

image.caption: Sam Altman, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer, OpenAI, testifies before a Senate Committee in 2025. Altman is facing 37 lawsuits related to the Tumbler Ridge school shooting. (Jose Luis Magana/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
Lawyers for OpenAI claim any legal action related to the deaths and injuries should take place in British Columbia.
Tech giant argues British Columbia is best place for legal battle over mass shooting responsibility

OpenAI wants a U.S. judge to dismiss more than three dozen lawsuits filed in California by survivors and families of victims of the Tumbler Ridge school shooting who claim the tech giant and its chief executive officer could have prevented the tragedy.
In motions to dismiss some of the 37 U.S. federal court actions, lawyers for OpenAI claim any legal action related to the deaths and injuries should take place in British Columbia.

The company says it will ultimately defend itself against what it calls "baseless accusations" but insists both private and public interests would be best served by putting the case in front of a B.C. judge.
"California is not the most appropriate forum for claims by British Columbians attacked by a British Columbian in British Columbia," the motion to dismiss reads.

"British Columbia plainly is an available and adequate alternative forum, so the key questions ... are where the parties can access evidence and which forum has the greater interest. The answer to both is British Columbia."

items: More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: On Feb. 10, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people — including six children — before taking her own life.
Questions about the shooter's interactions with the health care system and police arose in the wake of the tragedy — turning to OpenAI after news reports about Van Rootselaar's use of ChatGPT.
The first lawsuits filed against OpenAI and CEO Altman were filed last spring in California, where the company is headquartered, with another wave of claims following earlier this month.
The claims alleged "ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it."

items: Teachers, students file new wave of lawsuits against OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge shooting

blocks.text: The victims claim the company flagged the shooter's ChatGPT account for "gun violence and planning" eight months before the attack, but "after a contentious internal debate, made the conscious decision not to warn authorities."

They claim to be suing both Altman and his company "for designing a dangerous product, ignoring the warnings of their own safety team, refusing to notify authorities when they knew the shooter was planning a mass attack, inviting them back onto the platform after deactivating their account, and choosing profit over the lives of the children of Tumbler Ridge."
Lawyer for Tumbler Ridge victims says OpenAI should be held accountable
'Forum non conveniens'

OpenAI has filed identical motions to dismiss a number of the suits over the past two weeks, citing a legal concept called "forum non conveniens" to argue that British Columbia is the logical place to bring any legal action related to the Tumbler Ridge shooting.
The company says most of the evidence in the case is in British Columbia as are most of the people likely to serve as witnesses.
OpenAI also says B.C has a "uniquely strong sovereign interest in having these actions resolved at home."

The motion to dismiss claims the court actions will require an examination of the role of "Canadian law enforcement, firearms regulations and British Columbia institutions in the events that preceded the shooting."
OpenAI says the actions would overlap "with Canada’s ongoing examination of its own institutions and policy choices."

"The jury may need to determine, among other questions, whether Canadian law enforcement acted reasonably in returning guns to the home of a mentally unstable teenager who had recently committed arson in an attempt to kill her family and had repeatedly been involuntarily hospitalized under British Columbia’s mental health legislation," the court document reads.
"The standard of care may turn on Canadian and British Columbia statutes and community practices — which differ from those in California."
Claims are 'not viable'
Wherever the lawsuits eventually take place, OpenAI says it intends to fight the allegations.

"[The] legal claims — blaming OpenAI for a horrific mass shooting by a deeply troubled teenager after systemic failures by the law enforcement, mental-health care, and educational institutions in her community — are not viable" the motion to dismiss says.

"Nor are the claims against Samuel Altman, who was not personally involved in the June 2025 review of the shooter’s ChatGPT account or the decision at that time not to refer her account to Canadian law enforcement."

items: 'My students should be here': Tumbler Ridge teacher shares toll of deadly school shooting

blocks.text: In the wake of revelations about the shooter's ChatGPT history, Altman apologized to the Tumbler Ridge community and said the company has updated its protocols.
The B.C. government is also planning legal action against OpenAI, and has since demolished the site of Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jason Proctor is a reporter in British Columbia for CBC News who has covered the B.C. courts and justice system extensively.

articles.title: ‘Outright racist’ activist Daniel Thomas will face ‘full force of law’ over any crimes, says home secretary
articles.summary:
Shabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sites

Shabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas…

blocks.text: Shabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington.

In an interview with the Guardian, the home secretary also “wanted to reassure” concerned villagers that asylum seekers due to move in to a neighbouring former defence site would not “put pressure” on local resources because they would be given “self-contained facilities”.

Her intervention came after Thomas, a convicted criminal known as “Danny Tommo” and the co-founder of the Patriot Platform, said thousands of his masked followers could descend “for days” on to the Oxfordshire village to prevent male asylum seekers being moved in.

At the launch of a crackdown on knife crime in Birmingham on Thursday, Mahmood said she wanted to distinguish between legitimate concerns felt by Piddington residents over a large-scale asylum centre and extremists who were “hijacking” community concerns.

“I understand the anxiety of local people when they’re about to see a change to their community. But it is important to distinguish that anxiety, where reasonable people can have a conversation, and the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas walking into town, hijacking an issue and then using that to divide our communities,” she said.
“Their behaviour is completely unacceptable. And where they break the law, they will face the full force of the law.”

blocks.caption: Residents of Piddington, Oxfordshire, voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic ‘referendum’.  Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: Piddington’s local population registered their opposition to the proposed asylum facility on Wednesday, casting 285 votes against 26 in a symbolic ballot to leave the UK and seek self-determination.

The parish has been approached by hundreds of other town and village councillors and residents for advice on replicating the campaign, which was backed by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats.
Thomas visited Piddington the day after the vote. He was dressed in a grey suit and white shirt and was not accompanied by people wearing balaclavas.
Joe Marshall, a parish councillor, said it was a private visit and Thomas was due to be given a tour of the village and a cup of tea by a resident.

“It is a closed meeting. We will engage with them and walk them around the village and have a cup of tea,” he said. “We have also had an open invitation to Reform, Labour, Conservatives and Restore to visit.”
Marshall said it was not clear that villagers would want security assistance from men in balaclavas, if it were offered. “This is a mild-mannered place,” he said.

blocks.caption: Piddington, Oxfordshire; MoD Bicester, the proposed site for the asylum camp, can be seen in the background. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: Thomas visited the village hall briefly and later visited the entrance to the Ministry of Justice camp where the asylum seekers are scheduled to be housed. In an interview broadcast on YouTube with Dan Wootton, he said he had spoken to three residents.

“The people we are meeting are just normal mothers, normal grandmothers, normal men,” Thomas said. “We have to start somewhere. Right now there are no men in that camp. We are going to put a legal, lawful plan in place to help this community in a way that has never been done before.”

Asked how she would respond to Piddington residents after the vote, Mahmood said: “I want to reassure the residents of Piddington that actually our experience from other large sites where we already have, asylum seekers accommodated, whether that’s in Wethersfield or Crowborough, is that putting all facilities on to one site is actually the best way to manage pressures for local communities.

“Our experience of other large sites where we are housing asylum seekers is that we’re able to put on that site more of the facilities that asylum seekers need. It’s a relatively self-contained facility, and the knock-on pressure to those local areas, I don’t think we’re going to see.”

Mahmood said she understood the anxiety of people in the countryside towards large groups of asylum seekers, but she pointed out that many people in inner-city areas such as her Birmingham constituency had similar concerns.

“I do understand the anxiety that people feel, when they’re about to see a change in their community or they are reading misinformation on the internet, or when they’re just concerned that a village is about to have a facility nearby that maybe they think may pose them some challenges,” she said.

“I also hear that concern from communities such as mine, where there are large numbers of HMOs [houses of multiple occupation] and accommodation in which asylum seekers are held as well. There is concern across every type of community. Not just in the countryside or in those sorts of areas, but in inner-city areas as well.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Shabana Mahmood said she understood ‘the anxiety of local people when they’re about to see a change to their community’. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA

blocks.text: Thomas and his supporters recently coordinated disruptive protests in Dover and Portsmouth, where masked supporters blocked roads and attempted to intercept newly arrived people.

On Thursday, Mahmood summoned police chiefs and urged them to improve their intelligence gathering and use all powers at their disposal, including new laws that allow for a blanket ban on face coverings at a designated location.
Hampshire police then sought to impose the ban on Saturday as an anti-asylum demonstration took place in Thomas’s home town of Portsmouth. Thomas urged his supporters to stay away.
A former bodyguard for Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, Thomas established his anti-immigration movement after serving a prison sentence for attempted kidnapping.

In an interview with Robinson, broadcast on Friday night, he said: “How powerful would it be if 5,000 men … surround the [Piddington] camp. We take tents. We sit there for days and we don’t let them [the asylum seekers] get in. And then we reinforce [the blockade] with members from the north, from Scotland, from Ireland.”

In the interview, Thomas said he was not racist and welcomed people of other nationalities into his organisation. “Racism within our organisation is just not acceptable. That is the stance we have. We are not a white nationalist movement. I have friends that are black.”
Thomas has been approached for comment.

Mahmood made her comments as she launched an anti-knife crime programme. More than 230 areas affected by knife crime will share £26.25m to pay for police patrols, CCTV and early-prevention work as part of a knife-crime crackdown across 27 police forces in England and Wales.

Each area, roughly the size of 10 football pitches, will receive more police patrols, alongside programmes designed for young people most at risk of being a victim or a perpetrator of knife crime. Action in small, targeted areas was the most effective way of driving down knife crime, the Home Office said.

Mahmood launched the initiative at the Acocks Green boxing gym in south Birmingham, which plays a role in the local area in supporting vulnerable young people to stay away from crime. She was joined by the anti-knife campaigners Lynne Baird, Lorraine Jones Burrell and Pooja Kanda. Each has lost a child to knife crime.
Additional reporting by Amelia Gentleman

articles.title: Fact check: Viral Duterte video after ICC appearance is AI-generated
articles.summary: The video appears to show the ex-president thanking supporters and asking for prayers for Sara.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 7:00am

MANILA, Philippines — A viral video supposedly showing former President Rodrigo Duterte thanking his supporters after personally appearing before the International Criminal Court (ICC) is AI-generated.
A TikTok user shared the video on Wednesday, September 16, showing Duterte allegedly thanking his supporters and asking them to include his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, in their prayers.

"Isama ninyo sa inyong mga panalangin ang aking anak na si Inday. Ipagdasal ninyo sana na bigyan siya ng Diyos ng lakas, tapang, at karunungan upang malampasan niya ang lahat ng pagsubok na kanyang kinakaharap ngayon," the AI-generated video of Duterte said.
(Include my daughter Inday in your prayers. Please pray that God gives her the strength, courage and wisdom to overcome all the challenges she is facing.)
The same video was posted earlier by Facebook page Edd AI at around 7:18 p.m., more than two hours before it was shared by the TikTok user at around 9:29 p.m.
The Facebook page also included a disclaimer saying its content was AI-generated, along with the hashtags #aigenerated and #satire.
Duterte appeared in person before the ICC for the first time on September 16 for the third status conference in his case.
He previously appeared before the court via videolink during his initial appearance in March 2025.
— Voiced by Philstar.com / Janelle Liong Script and editing by Philstar.com / Geraldine Santos

articles.title: Far-right German politician heckles Carney with 'U.S.A.' chant before EU address
articles.summary: As Prime Minister Mark Carney approached the podium at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, he was met by a lone heckler with an unexpected chant for a Canadian leader speaking to the EU in France.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers an address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
As Prime Minister Mark Carney approached the podium at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, he was met by a lone heckler with an unexpected chant for a Canadian leader speaking to the EU in France.
German MEP says chant was meant to address 'elephant in the room'
"U.S.A.! U.S.A.!" German MEP Siegbert Droese called out.
Some in the crowd groaned, then Carney chuckled and carried on with his speech where he called for closer ties between Canada and the EU and an "alliance for the future."
In a statement provided to CBC News, Droese said the chant was his way of "addressing the geopolitical elephant in the room."
‘U.S.A., U.S.A.': German politician chants as Carney speaks to EU Parliament
Droese said Carney's reaction to his callout shows the prime minister "clearly has a sense of humor."

Carney's address to the Parliament in Strasbourg is just another step in a bilateral push for a tightened relationship with the EU and comes just a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the bloc's first "associate member" — a new, and as of yet, undefined title.

items: Read Mark Carney's full speech to the European Parliament
What we know about the proposed partnership between Canada and the EU

blocks.text: "It was an absurd and unrealistic knee-jerk reaction for Ms. von der Leyen to propose an 'associate EU membership' for Canada: a status not provided for in any of the European treaties," Droese wrote in his statement.
Droese is a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been surging in popularity among German voters.

The AfD's domestic policies include proposing large-scale deportations of anyone of non-German heritage and a push for what the party calls a patriotic cultural policy to cut funding for projects not deemed suitably national — such as some Holocaust remembrance programs.
In his statement, Droese called the European Commission president corrupt and suggested she's seeking an agreement with Canada to bypass her "abysmal" relations with the U.S.
Droese ended his statement by saying there is a "certain irony in the fact that the six letters 'USA! USA!' were enough" to trigger a reaction.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Man who sprayed Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months
articles.summary:
Anthony Kazmierczak agreed plea deal over January town-hall attack that came amid Minneapolis ICE crackdown

The man who

blocks.text: The man who sprayed vinegar at the Democratic US House member Ilhan Omar during a Minneapolis town hall was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison after reaching a deal with prosecutors.

The sentencing of 56-year-old Anthony Kazmierczak came nearly eight months after the 27 January assault. At the time, Minneapolis was facing an immigration crackdown that led to angry protests, arrests and the killing of two US citizens by federal officers.
Kazmierczak was also sentenced to three years of supervised release, which includes no contact with Omar. US marshals escorted him from the courtroom after he was sentenced.
“This wasn’t a spur-of-the-moment act,” the US district judge Joan N Ericksen said before handing down the sentence, noting that Kazmierczak had secured tickets for the town hall weeks in advance.

“An attack on a public figure is not a political statement. It is misguided, selfish and inconsistent with any concept of a free or democratic society,” Ericksen added. She also said spraying anything at an elected official “is a terrifying thing. And you knew that when you did it.”

Kazmierczak, who has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, shook visibly at times as he sat at the defense table. He spoke quietly and haltingly, occasionally wiping away tears as he stood before Ericksen.

He spoke about being a good neighbor – and how his troubles with insurance companies as well as prison had exacerbated his ailments. His attorney, John Fossum, argued that Kazmierczak had not been taking his mental health medications before the attack, lowering his inhibitions and contributing to what happened.
“I’ve spent enough time in jail thinking,” Kazmierczak said, his voice barely audible. “I really apologize to her for having put her through that,” he said, referring to Omar.
In an earlier hearing, Kazmierczak was unable to explain his actions, saying only “it’s fuzzy” when Ericksen asked what he remembered.
“I’m sorry if I scared you,” he wrote to Omar after the attack.

During the town hall, witnesses saw Kazmierczak jump up from the audience, spraying liquid from a syringe at Omar and saying she was “splitting Minnesota apart”. Omar’s security officers tackled Kazmierczak and turned him over to police, who arrested him.
Omar was not injured and continued with the town hall after the arrest.
Authorities later determined he had sprayed her with a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a US officer.
after newsletter promotion

The government sentencing memorandum, submitted to the court by prosecutors, said he had texted at least three people indicating he planned to do something at the meeting involving Omar “but would not answer their questions about his intent”.
He also sent messages to a neighbor to arrange for dog care and asking for bail bond company contact information.

The sentencing memo said Kazmierczak had long struggled with alcohol abuse and had “a history of mental and emotional health concerns” and a string of health issues tied to his 2022 Parkinson’s disease diagnosis.

Omar, a refugee from Somalia, has long been a target of Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant rhetoric across his two presidencies. In 2019, after Omar’s election to Congress, Trump said she should “go back” to her country of birth. He has described her as “garbage” and said she should be investigated.

In social media posts, Kazmierczak had criticized Joe Biden – who was president between Trump’s two Oval Office terms – and referred to Democrats as “angry and liars”. He wrote that Trump wants the US to be “stronger and more prosperous”.
His attack came as the Minneapolis area was on edge due to the crackdown, with protesters often facing off against convoys of immigration officers and conservatives criticizing protesters.

articles.title: YouTube star Ms Rachel to match Macklemore’s $1m Palestine aid donation
articles.summary:
Educator talks of ‘moral obligation’ and urges ‘every wealthy white celebrity’ to make similar donation

YouTube star

blocks.text: YouTube star Ms Rachel has said she is matching rapper Macklemore’s $1m donation to organizations supporting Palestinians, calling on other public figures to follow suit.

Macklemore, who was fired as the opening act on Ed Sheeran’s tour after saying “Free Palestine” on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, pledged to donate the entirety of his earnings from Sheeran’s tour to several organizations focused on the Palestinian people.
Ms Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote on Instagram: “Over 20,000 precious Palestinian children have been killed, and children continue to be killed every day.”
Accurso said her donation would go to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund.
“We have a moral obligation to use our privilege and platforms to protect children and human rights,” she wrote.

Accurso, a children’s entertainer with over 21 million YouTube subscribers, has been vocal about the hardships Gaza’s young people face amid the war with Israel. She encouraged “every wealthy white celebrity” to match her donation.
Accurso is the latest public figure to back Macklemore, after he was dropped from Sheeran’s Loop tour for remarks he made at a 4 September concert about the plight of the Palestinian people.
“Free Palestine! I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he said during a two-minute speech.

Macklemore’s words prompted a flurry of criticism from Israel-aligned groups. The singer Pink also called on Macklemore to be removed from the tour, and referenced a 2014 incident where he wore a costume decried for bearing resemblance to Jewish caricature. Macklemore apologized for the costume at the time.

Pink expanded on her position in an Instagram post, saying she was not speaking on behalf of the Israeli government, but rather wanted to advocate for Jewish concertgoers who may have been alarmed by the rapper’s remarks.

Macklemore directly addressed Jewish audience members at a second tour date on 5 September, saying: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”
Sheeran has maintained the decision to fire Macklemore was led by stadium owners, including Gillette Stadium and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft.

Sheeran wrote on Tuesday on Instagram: “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”
Kraft and Sheeran are both donating $2m each to Palestinian relief funds, Kraft said Wednesday, although it is unclear which organizations their funds will support.
Four supporting acts, among them American singer Finneas and Danish pop band Lukas Graham, have quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.

articles.title: Trump hails 'major progress' in setting up US base in Poland
articles.summary: The location of the permanent US military base in Poland could be announced "very soon," Donald Trump has said. The US president also praised the leadership of his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki.

image.caption: Karol Nawrocki (left) visited the White House last year. During the visit, Trump offered to send more US troops to Poland [FILE: September 3, 2025]Image: Aaron Schwartz/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that significant progress had been made toward establishing a US military base in Poland.
"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
In August, Warsaw revealed that it was in talks with Washington regarding a permanent US military presence in Poland.
"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance," Trump added in a social media post.

His announcement comes despite his administration's launch of a formal review of its military presence in Europe. This has raised fears among allies that the US could reduce its military presence there.
How did Warsaw react?
Nawrocki, who is a conservative ally of the US president, thanked Trump on X, saying Poland was "ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation."
He added, "I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base."

Meanwhile, Zbigniew Bogucki, the head of the Polish president's chancellery, called Trump's announcement "great news for Poland." He also noted that it came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland.
In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said his country was discussing with the United States the possibility of establishing a permanent US base on its territory.
"We have already completed the initial stage of the process, not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told the public broadcaster TVP.
Can Poland hold NATO’s line against Russia without the US?
Poland secures NATO's eastern flank
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been pushing for a larger allied presence on NATO's eastern flank.
Nearly 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland, a member of both NATO and the EU. However, they are there almost exclusively on a rotational basis.

Poland's proximity to Ukraine and Russia is a key factor in its security strategy. The country allocates approximately 5% of its gross domestic product to defense spending and has been working to increase the United States' military presence.
In the meantime, Washington heavily criticized several European countries for refusing to allow US forces to use NATO bases in its war with Iran.

articles.title: More than 500,000 Albertans have applied to vote by mail in referendum: Elections Alberta
articles.summary: More than half a million Albertans have requested to vote by mail in the upcoming referendum, according to Elections Alberta.

image.caption: Elections Alberta has received more than 509,000 requests for special mail-in ballots ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum. The deadline to apply to vote by mail is Friday, Sept. 25. (Janet French/CBC News)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
More than half a million Albertans have requested to vote by mail in the upcoming referendum, according to Elections Alberta.
Agency still looking for thousands of people to work the referendum
More than half a million Albertans have applied to vote by mail in the upcoming referendum, according to Elections Alberta.
An agency spokesperson told CBC News Thursday it has received more than 509,000 requests for special ballots, with eight days left for electors to apply for that voting method.

Elections Alberta has known for weeks that there was greater demand to vote by mail in the referendum scheduled for Oct. 19. But the number of requests received so far is already more than eight times greater than the roughly 60,000 special ballots requested in the 2023 provincial election.

The Oct. 19 referendum features 10 questions on a variety of issues. Most notably, the list includes a question about whether Alberta should remain in Canada or whether the provincial government should start the process to hold a binding referendum on secession.

items: Special mail-in ballot requests surge above 175,000 ahead of Alberta referendum

blocks.text: Elections Alberta also says it's working with jails and prisons to ensure inmates can vote. Incarcerated Albertans vote through mail-in ballots.
The agency couldn't say how many inmates have requested ballots for the referendum, but it said just over 400 applied to vote in the 2023 election.
LISTEN | What to know about mail-in ballots ahead of Oct. 19:
Calgary Eyeopener11:09What you need to know about special mail-in ballots ahead of October's referendum

The Correctional Service of Canada says staff have been ensuring inmates are aware of their right to vote and that posters about the upcoming referendum have been put up throughout institutions in Alberta.
There are almost three million eligible voters in the province, according to Elections Alberta, meaning about 17 per cent have expressed intentions to vote by mail in this election.
The last provincial referendum, in 2021, saw voter turnout of about 39 per cent.
Elections Alberta gaining recruits
Elections Alberta is also making headway toward having the number of people it needs for referendum day.
The agency set out to recruit 60,000 electoral workers. It has launched a recruitment campaign and even solicited electoral management bodies in other parts of Canada to help out.

items: Elections Alberta soliciting help from other jurisdictions to carry out fall referendum

blocks.text: A spokesperson said that, as of Thursday, almost 48,000 people have applied to be election officers. They didn't have a total number of how many were hired.
