articles.title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
articles.summary: There is no certainty that the idea will ever get off the ground, let alone become a blueprint for other countries, writes Katya Adler.

blocks.text: Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.
The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.

But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."
Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.

The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.
Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.
The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else.

"We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right.
Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.

This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.
Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.

Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act".
But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in.
Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU.

But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs.
They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence.

Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too.
For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships.

But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership.
Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries.
No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example.
A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU.
Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc.

In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

articles.title: ‘Cocaine eyes’ to cash bribes: 5 revelations from Project South wiretaps

image.caption: Const. Timothy Barnhardt is facing a long list of charges in connection with allegedly assisting organized crime. (@10rcop/X)

blocks.text: A police officer doing drugs before his shift, a trunk of police uniforms to sell, details on drug deals and plans to open massage parlours are some of the revelations Project South investigators allegedly captured through wiretaps as part of their sweeping corruption probe, according to newly reportable details from an Information to Obtain (ITO) application in the case.
A publication ban was lifted on those allegations, and many others, from the Project South ITO this week in a ruling from Ontario Superior Court Justice Laura Bird.

“The importance of public scrutiny in this case cannot be overstated. What is, perhaps, most concerning about the allegations of widespread police corruption in this case is the fact that the York Regional Police only stumbled upon it in the course of their investigation,” wrote Bird in her decision.

The investigation began in June 2025, when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections official from Toronto South Detention Centre (TSDC). Subsequently, police discovered that Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt allegedly ran an unauthorized search on the official's licence plate less than a month before the attempted hit.
“There is no evidence that anyone was suspicious of Mr. Barnhardt or his associates until that moment," Bird wrote.
"That is something that should be of tremendous concern to the public because it demonstrates that a trusted public official can engage in widespread illegal conduct and go undetected.”
CBC News was part of a group of media organizations fighting to lift a publication ban on the ITO — which lays out months' worth of evidence police had compiled from wiretaps and other warrants.

The allegations in the ITO have not been tested in court, but many of the conversations intercepted by investigators paint a picture of the corruption investigators allege Barnhardt and other Toronto police officers and civilians engaged in over several months in 2025 and early this year before their arrests.
These are five of the most shocking conversations police intercepted.
Going to daycare with ‘cocaine eyes’

In early October 2025, investigators intercepted Barnhardt buying cocaine from Const. Saurabjit Bedi in a Brampton, Ont., plaza, according to the ITO. Barnhardt’s vehicle was bugged with audio and video recording devices and investigators say the pair are “seen and heard weighing out the drugs and can be heard negotiating a price of $230 for Barnhardt to pay.”
Afterward, Bedi called Barnhardt and the following exchange was captured, according to the portions of transcript in the ITO.
Bedi asked Barnhardt if he “looked f--ked up when you saw me? … cuz I’m going to daycare now.”
Barnhard replied: “Just put your sunglasses on that’s all, you got … what do they call them … cocaine eyes.”
From there police say the pair discussed drug dosages.
In December 2025, the ITO said police also observed Bedi “consuming what appeared to be cocaine” in the parking lot of 12 Division before starting his shift.

Both Barnhardt and Bedi are charged with trafficking cocaine. None of the charges against them have been tested in court yet. Barnhardt’s lawyer declined to comment on allegations from the ITO and Bedi’s did not respond to a request for comment.

items: Toronto cop charged in Project South allegedly didn't care if selling information harmed people

blocks.text: ‘All they want is protection’
Police intercepted Barnhardt and Bedi drinking and doing drugs in late November 2025 while discussing plans for a marijuana dispensary and a massage parlour, according to the ITO.
Bedi explained to Barnhardt that he has “girls,” and “all they want is protection and safety and we get their cuts.” He also allegedly told Barnhardt it would be better to use hotels.

items: Inmate and jail guard investigated, but not charged in Project South alleged murder plot

blocks.text: Investigators say Barnhardt then clarified to Bedi he was not talking about escorts, but rather massage parlours.
Both men are charged with conspiracy to obstruct justice and breach of trust.
‘What about all this s--t in the f--cking trunk man?’

In late October 2025, investigators intercepted a meeting between Barnhardt and civilian Brian Da Costa in Barnhardt’s vehicle. Da Costa is the one who allegedly paid Barnhardt to “routinely” run unauthorized database searches, including the one on the senior corrections official.
But on this night, the ITO says Da Costa paid Barnhardt cash for police uniform items that Barnhardt had in his trunk.
This is a transcript of the conversation included in the ITO:
Barnhardt: "What about all this s--t in the f--king trunk man…?"
Da Costa: "Oh s--t yeah my bad f--k; I forgot for a second what you were trying to hand me."

Barnhardt: "I'm like what the f--k 36, 38, 40 are the pants, and the f--king NCO pants are in here too, there is like 1, 2 ,3 jackets.... l got the other jacket I just gotta pick up with the toque and everything."
Da Costa: "I might qet a couple of bucks for this s--t and get more, okay?"
Barnhardt: "I’m gonna get you the hats and ball caps."
Da Costa: "We gotta go get the badges and s--t okay?"
Then, police said Da Costa was observed handing money to Barnhardt, while counting each bill aloud.
Da Costa: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, 10."
Barnhardt: "You are the f--king best, man."
Both men are charged with trafficking police uniforms. Da Costa remains in custody. His lawyer declined a request for comment on the ITO allegations.
Barnhardt jokes about visiting massage parlour daily
In early September 2025, Da Costa was intercepted asking Barnhardt if he wanted to partner with him opening a massage parlour, according to the ITO.
Barnhardt: "Oh f--k bro I’ve been trying to do that myself ... l just didn’t have the link for the women" [...] “I’ll put all my effort towards that, f--k it, a hundred percent.... I'm excited."
Da Costa allegedly jokes about receiving free services at the proposed massage parlour, to which the ITO says Barnhardt replied he would be there daily.
‘Inflammatory’ conversation still under pub ban
There is one conversation transcript in the ITO that Justice Bird decided to keep under a pub ban. It involves Barnhardt and Da Costa.
“The comments attributed to Mr. Barnhardt are particularly inflammatory and memorable,” wrote Bird in her decision.
“I am satisfied that they are the type of comments that could create an indelible impression of guilt in the minds of potential jurors that could not be dealt with by resort to alternative measures.”

Elsewhere in the ITO, CBC News previously reported that police say Barnhardt “explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed” as a result of information he sold to Da Costa from database searches.
This ITO was used by police to obtain more than 50 search warrants in the Project South investigation in early February.

The search warrants were executed as investigators arrested and charged seven Toronto police officers, one retired cop and 19 civilians in Project South. The charge against one of those civilians has since been stayed, and one of the officers retired and pleaded guilty to two charges in July.
The charges against the others accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court.

articles.title: A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
articles.summary: Fuel shortages, drone strikes and mobilization rumors are fueling anxiety and war fatigue in Russia. As support for peace talks grows among Russians, the Kremlin is watching closely ahead of…

image.caption: The upcoming Duma elections are hard to miss when you walk down Moscow's streetsImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russians are increasingly anxious. Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them.
According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan, 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives.
"Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW.

She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections.

blocks.caption: All 450 seats in the Duma are at stake in the upcoming electionImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sociologist and the founder of ExtremeScan Elena Koneva said people were starting to ask the question: "How much does this war cost me and my family? And am I ready to pay this price? "
That could pose a problem for the Kremlin.

From September 18 to 20, Russians are voting for a new parliament (the State Duma) for the first time since 2022. It's the first parliamentary election to take place in Russia during the Ukraine war. And although there are unlikely to be any surprises in the official results, the Kremlin will be closely monitoring turnout.
Why are these elections important for the Kremlin?
"The Kremlin is confident it can fabricate whatever figures it needs. The question is how high of a price it will have to pay," said Zavadskaya.

Although elections in authoritarian systems like that of Russian President Vladimir Putin have little to do with democratic change, they still serve an important purpose. They are a reality check on whether the population remains loyal. And for Putin, that is especially important right now.

"They are crucial for him because they demonstrate that the majority supports the main party, the party of war, and that he has legitimacy for further escalation and the continuation of this war," Russian opposition politician in exile Ilya Yashin told DW.

In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, there is little sign the Kremlin is willing to end the conflict. United Russia, a party de facto led by Putin, is campaigning on a platform that lists victory in the war among its priorities. Its candidate list is headed by people presented as veterans of the war against Ukraine.
But many Russians appear to want the opposite.

"The silent majority just wants the war to end," opposition politician Yulia Galyamina, who still lives in Russia, said in a recent interview with online media-outlet Bereg. Most of these people still support Putin, but they are becoming increasingly anti-war, she said.

That mood is also reflected in polling. Six in 10 Russians favor peace negotiations with Ukraine, according to independent pollster Levada Center. Recent Kremlin hints at a new round of peace talks in October may be a tactic to calm the electorate, Zavadskaya said.
Support for Yabloko has been rising
One party has sought to capitalize on this anti-war sentiment: Yabloko.
The liberal opposition party is the only registered political force opposing the war in Ukraine.
Although its rating was below 5% in July, the party has seen a surge in popularity since then. Many people, especially younger Russians, are joining Yabloko and volunteering.
Russian court confirms anti-war party election ban

According to the independent pollster ExtremeScan, 18% of Russians would have voted for Yabloko. But they will not be able to: In a recent court decision, Yabloko was barred from running in the parliamentary elections.
"This support for Yabloko is, in fact, a demonstration of people's attitude toward the war," Koneva told DW.
What will anti-war voters do?
Now, with Yabloko out of the race, are there still ways for Russians to express that attitude?

Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Alexei Navalny, and opposition politician in exile Maxim Katz are urging supporters to back any party except United Russia in an effort to reduce the ruling party's result in the election.
Yabloko has taken a different approach, encouraging voters to spoil their ballots.
Yashin says neither choice matters. What matters, he says, is showing up at polling stations at noon on Sept. 20.

blocks.caption: Navalnaya (center) and Yashin (right) have different suggestions for how voters in Russia can show their discontent with the government (file photo from June 2025)Image: Alexis Haulot/European Union 2025 - Source : EP

blocks.text: "These queues will be a visible expression of public discontent," he said. "No need for flags, banners, or symbols. Everyone will know: the queues at noon are made up of people who do not want the war to continue."
DW Russian asked its readers anonymously whether they plan to vote in the upcoming election. Most of those who responded said they would follow Navalnaya's and Katz's advice.
"Elections have long become a farce and a political spectacle. But I will vote because I want to show that I have a position," one user said.
Others decided to stay away from the elections. One respondent wrote: "I don't want to legitimize Putin's regime."
Sergei Satanovskii contributed reporting.

articles.title: Germany: Third malaria death linked to Frankfurt Airport
articles.summary: Two new malaria cases have been registered this week near Frankfurt airport, two months after cases first emerged.

image.caption: Thee malaria cases were attributed to a mosquito that arrived at Frankfurt Airport inside an aircraft.Image: James Gathany/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A person living near the Schwanheim district of Frankfurt died of malaria, local authorities said on Thursday. The incident is the third such death after a recent cluster of malaria cases linked to Frankfurt Airport emerged.
Two airport workers died of the disease in July and August.
Malaria is a life-threatening disease transmitted by mosquitoes and causes hundreds of thousands of deaths per year, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is not common in Germany.

Schwanheim district, which borders the airport, registered two new malaria cases on Tuesday this week. Neither of the two infected individuals, both living in different households, had previously visited a malaria-endemic area and they did not work at Frankfurt airport.

Frankfurt health authorities extended their condolences to the relatives of the latest victims and said the two latest cases in the Schwanheim district were linked to an infected Anopheles mosquito that arrived in Germany by plane.

Germany's public health institute, the Robert Koch Institute, said malaria mosquitoes can fly between 5 and 10 kilometers (3 to 6 miles). The registered infections occurred some 5 kilometers away from the airport.
What is airport malaria?
Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad. But in this instance, the cases are attributed directly to Frankfurt Airport.
Airport malaria can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area.
The RKI describes such cases as very rare, with the last documented case at Frankfurt Airport having been recorded in 2023.
Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual.
Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin.
Still, Frankfurt Airport urged employees at the airport to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms.
Malaria research in Germany targets parasite’s life cycle

articles.title: Alexander Ovechkin backs Putin party in campaign video
articles.summary: Ice hockey legend Alexander Ovechkin has lent Vladimir Putin's party a helping hand in its parliamentary election campaign. That's in keeping with a pattern of support by an athlete who claims not to…

image.caption: Alexander Ovechkin is set to play his 22nd season in the NHLImage: IMAGO/ITAR-TASS

blocks.text: When Russia's parliamentary elections are held from September 18 to 20, Alexander Ovechkin won't be there to cast his ballot in person. On Monday he took his first few strides back on the ice in the United States as he starts gearing up for a new National Hockey League (NHL) season with the Washington Capitals, his 22nd in the world's best league.

Before leaving his homeland, where he spent his summer break, he did make his contribution to the election campaign, however, appearing in a video promoting the ruling United Russia party, which steadfastly supports President Vladimir Putin.

In the video, which has been widely shared on social media, Ovechkin doesn't speak but can be clearly seen in the third row of a group of supporters behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who is heading the United Russia list for the parliamentary vote.

Ovechkin's appearance has faced criticism, including from Ukrainian skeleton pilot Vladyslav Heraskevych, who was disqualified from the 2026 Olympic Games for insisting on wearing a helmet depicting athletes killed in Russia's war in Ukraine.
Ovechkin a long-standing Putin supporter
This is certainly not the first time that Ovechkin has expressed his support for Putin, with whom he shares his profile photo on his Instagram account.

blocks.caption: Ovechkin's Instagram account features a profile photo of him with PutinImage: @aleksandrovechkinofficial/instagram

blocks.text: And, at times, Ovechkin's public support has appeared even more active than in the current United Russia video. Back in 2017, Ovechkin used his Instagram account to announce the creation of "PutinTeam" a group to help support Putin in the 2018 presidential campaign.

"I have never hidden my feelings about our president; I have always openly supported him. I am certain there are many of us who support Vladimir Putin! So let's unite and show the world a strong, united Russia!" he wrote.
"Being part of such a team is a source of pride for me; it feels just like pulling on the Russian national team jersey, knowing the whole country is rooting for you."

The creation of PutinTeam came three years after Russia had invaded and seized the Ukrainian territory Crimea in 2014, a move that was met with widespread condemnation in the international community. Later that year, Ovechkin appeared to express support for the operation, posting a photo of himself on Instagram holding up a sign with the message: "#savechildrenfromfascism."
"Our grandfathers and grandmothers witnessed all the horrors of fascism! We will not let it happen in our time," he wrote.

Putin has painted the Ukrainian authorities as "neo-Nazi" or fascist, in particular when justifying Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022. What Putin calls a "special military operation" raised questions in the minds of many about how this might affect Ovechkin's view of the man he had always so publicly supported.
On February 25, 2022, a day after Russia launched the invasion, a reporter covering the Washington Capitals asked Ovechkin if he still supported Putin.
"Well, he's my president," Ovechkin replied. "But how I said, I'm not in politics, I'm an athlete."
He did issue a vague appeal for peace but declined to criticize Moscow's military action.
"Please, no more war. It doesn't matter who's in the war — Russia, Ukraine, different countries," he said.
Capitals: 'Ovechkin asked by his country'
Approached for comment on Tuesday, the NHL referred reporters to the Washington Capitals.
"Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who ‌lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will ‌live ​there following his retirement," team spokesperson Sergey Kocharov said in the statement.

"This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign. As the longest-tenured athlete in Washington, D.C., and a pillar of the community, his focus and ours is on the season ahead and the ⁠continued impact ​he makes on the ice and in our ​city."
'They asked me, I said yes, simple as that'
When Ovechkin was made available to reporters two days later, his message was essentially the same.

"About the video; I'm Russian. Once I finish playing hockey I am probably going to live there, my kids going to live there, my family. So I'm for peace and love and I hope everthing is going to be okay. My home is Russia," he said.
Asked by a reporter how he came to be involved in the campaign video, Ovechkin replied: "They asked me to do this and I said yes. Simple as that."
Back on the ice
Whatever you may think of his political views, Ovechkin is without a doubt one of the best players to ever lace on a pair of skates.

Now, back on the ice in Arlington, Virginia, ahead of the Washington Capitals' training camp, "Great8" is focused on getting his aging body (he turned 41 on Thursday) ready to compete for what would be a second Stanley Cup for both him and the Caps.

For much of the offseason, Ovechkin had left open whether he would return for another year. After all, he has achieved just about everything you can in the NHL, having broken Wayne Gretzky's career goal-scoring record two seasons ago. Going into the 2025-26 campaign he has 929 goals in 1,573 regular season games. In July though, after a conversation with his wife, he decided to come back for one more year in Washington – and he hasn't ruled out extending his career beyond that.
Over 40 and still going strong

"I'm going to be 41. I've had a lot of pressure on my shoulders over the years," he said. "I'm going to focus on the game and helping my team to win," he told reporters after his first skate. "I'm still a good player and can still help the team to win."
His numbers support that last assertion, having scored 32 goals in 2025-26. Only two other players have ever scored more over the age of 40.
"I can't wait for the season," he said. "On paper, you can see our team is one of the best teams but now we have to work for the Stanley Cup."
The bookies disagree, however, with some putting the Capitals way down at 18 (of 32) on their list of Stanley Cup candidates for 2027.
On the other hand, the prospect of United Russia's winning this weekend's parliamentary elections, the first since the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, appears a safe bet.
This article was originally published on September 15, 2026. It was updated on September 16 with the comment of the Capitals spokesmand and on September 17 with the comment of Ovechkin himself.

articles.title: More Pinoy couples use contraceptives – CPD
articles.summary: The number of Filipino couples engaging in family planning through the use of contraceptives is increasing, the Commission on Population and Development said.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 12:00am

“In 2022, there was a 41.8-percent increase and that in 2025, it went up to 44.5 percent. This means more Filipinos are practicing family planning,” CPD Information and Communication Management Division chief Mylin Mirasol Quiray said at the Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon program yesterday.
AFP / File
MANILA, Philippines — The number of Filipino couples engaging in family planning through the use of contraceptives is increasing, the Commission on Population and Development (CPD) said.
She pointed out that though there are still users of the traditional withdrawal as well as calendar method, the number of those using contraceptives is going up.
“The 2025 data showed the percentage of users of contraceptives are higher at 44.5 percent compared to those still into the traditional methods at 14.1 percent,” said Quiray.
She stressed the importance of family planning so that choices are made available to the women and their families.
Quiray also said that in areas where access to education and awareness on family planning to most women are limited, they continuously work with concerned local government units.
“We train LGUs to ensure there will be available services and information in their respective areas with regard to family planning,” she said.

World Contraception Day, which is observed annually every Sept. 26, aims to bring awareness on the availability of contraceptive methods and encourage people to make informed decisions concerning their sexual and reproductive health.

articles.title: Ridon, Tolosa ordered: Explain sub judice breach

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Rep. Terry Ridon and Atty. Benjamin Tolosa Jr.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui , House of Representatives

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court has ordered Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon and private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. to explain their perceived violations of the court’s sub judice rule.
With the receipt of the show-cause order, the House of Representatives’ prosecution team urged the impeachment court to also call out Vice President Sara Duterte.

Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong, one of the designated spokespersons in the impeachment trial, pointed out to journalists covering the proceedings that if presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero found some prosecutors to have committed such, then so has the Vice President.

“I think it should be applied universally. If we are really to set the standard for all parties involved in this impeachment trial to observe with due diligence, avoiding violating the sub judice rule, it would also be applied to the respondent herself,” he said, referring to Duterte.
Adiong noted that Duterte had openly declared her distrust of the court and even insinuated a presidential influence over it.
He described the remarks as attacks on the court itself.
Escudero issued the show-cause orders on Sept. 16.
The demand came after two prosecutors received orders to explain public statements that allegedly violated the court’s restrictions on discussing the pending case.
Ridon confirmed he was one of the two prosecutors issued the show-cause order.

articles.title: Evidence enough to convict VP, says prosecution
articles.summary: Documentary and testimonial evidence against impeached Vice President Sara Duterte are enough to convict her regardless of whether the conviction threshold is maintained or not, according to the…

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio
Facebook.com / Mayorindaysaraduterteofficial

MANILA, Philippines — Documentary and testimonial evidence against impeached Vice President Sara Duterte are enough to convict her regardless of whether the conviction threshold is maintained or not, according to the prosecution team of the House of Representatives.

“As far as we are concerned, we stick to the principle that we will sink or swim with the evidence that we will be presenting before the Senate impeachment court,” Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores (Bukidnon) – a member of the 11-member prosecution team – declared.
“Whether it’s 16, 14, or 13, we’re really just focused on presenting the evidence,” Flores said.
Akbayan Rep. Chel Diokno has repeatedly stressed that the prosecution’s focus is on the presentation of evidence and not on the voting threshold.
Flores said prosecutors have not yet finalized their collective position on the threshold issue tackled by a group of retired Supreme Court justice tapped as amici curiae or friends of the court.
“If there’s one thing that we don’t disagree on, it’s that the threshold is still two-thirds,” Flores said.
Rep. Joel Chua (Manila third district) also said they hope to secure a conviction for Duterte based on the strength of evidence.

“Whether it is 16, 15 or 14, we are preparing to show the extent of evidence that may hopefully convince the senator-judges that we have an overwhelming evidence that would warrant the conviction of the respondent,” he told reporters.

“At the end of the day, the audience here is not just limited to senator-judges, but to the entire Filipino population as well,” Chua, chairman of the House committee on good government and public accountability, emphasized.
The Constitution requires the concurrence of two-thirds of all Senate members for conviction.

With a 24-member Senate, presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero initially set the threshold at 16 votes, a decision that has sparked controversy because of non-participation of several senator-judges in trial proceedings – for various reasons.
The prosecution and defense are scheduled to argue their respective positions on the threshold on Sept. 23.
Sen. Rodante Marcoleta, currently detained for plunder, said he does not intend to seek furlough just so he could vote on the proposed change in 16-vote threshold.

“I will not move for a furlough just to vote for a threshold. I don’t think the threshold is a subject of a vote. It’s already in the Constitution. Nobody has a right to change the Constitution,” he said after the bail hearing on his plunder case. Also in detention for plunder is Sen. Jinggoy Estrada.

Two other senators, Loren Legarda and Ronald dela Rosa, are absent from the proceedings. Dela Rosa has been in hiding since May following the issuance of an arrest warrant against him by the International Criminal Court. Meanwhile, Legarda has been on an extended medical leave.
‘Indelible mark’

Reflecting on the appearance of former Supreme Court chief justices before the impeachment court last Wednesday, Sen. Panfilo Lacson said their expert testimonies have left an “indelible mark” on him and would guide him in the vote to resolve the conviction threshold.
Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III told reporters that senators would first hold a caucus before putting the threshold matter to a vote.
Malacañang, meanwhile, said it is keeping its hands off the issue. — Neil Jayson Servallos, Daphne Galvez, Alexis Romero

articles.title: Palace questions VP Sara’s capability to lead Philippines
articles.summary: Malacañang questioned the capability of Vice President Sara Duterte to lead the country after her camp claimed she is ready to succeed President Marcos.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 12:00am

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro says Vice President Sara Duterte's camp not listening seriously to Palace briefings, adds that is the reason why Duterte seems "clueless" about the administration's programs.
Screenshots / RTVM | via Alexis Romero
MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang questioned the capability of Vice President Sara Duterte to lead the country after her camp claimed she is ready to succeed President Marcos.

“Is that the reason why they are asking the President to resign immediately?” Palace press officer Claire Castro said in a media briefing yesterday. “That is normal and natural for allies of the Vice President, but whether she can succeed President Marcos, is this serious?”

Castro reiterated that demanding the resignation of Marcos without legal basis is “absolutely delusional,” as she assailed the statement of Paolo Panelo, the Vice President’s spokesman, that she is difficult to take seriously.
According to Castro, the remark was an admission that the Duterte camp is not listening to her statements about the programs and plans of the administration.

“Perhaps that is the reason why the Vice President seems to be clueless about the things that the administration is doing for our people. She always claims that nothing is being done. That is the reason: No time to listen, no time to watch and no time to listen seriously to what is being said, especially here in the briefings,” Castro said.

Meanwhile, Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong, one of the impeachment spokespersons, said Duterte should be the last person to call for Marcos’ resignation, amid alleged irregularities in government, out of delicadeza because she stands to benefit from it.

“I think for someone who has already indicated her desire to run for the presidency, I think she should be the last person to ask the sitting President to resign because that is entirely a political stand,” Adiong said.
“They don’t want the issues politicized and yet they’re the first ones politicizing everything,” he added.

During her postponed arraignment in a Quezon City court for charges of grave threats against the First Couple and former speaker Martin Romualdez last week, Duterte urged Marcos to resign, accusing his administration of corruption, abuse and political harassment.
Adiong said the issue is one of propriety because Duterte would be the direct beneficiary of a vacancy in the presidency.

“It is very, very clear who stands to benefit if the President steps down from office. It would of course be the VP, being the next in line to succeed if there’s a vacancy in the Office of the President,” Adiong said, adding that Duterte should not be leading calls for the President to step down. — Delon Porcalla

articles.title: All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan
articles.summary: Although Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that means

blocks.text: Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member.

Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One MEP leader described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion.

One day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued the unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an associate member – an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, who threatened Europe with “heavy tariffs” if it became a reality.

But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.”

The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship” but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”.
Merz himself has floated “associate membership” for Ukraine, as a stepping stone to joining the bloc, but this was quickly dismissed by other member states.

One EU diplomat said von der Leyen “seemed a bit far out in floating this” and that even before Wednesday’s speech member states had worried that she was overpromising on Canada. A second diplomat said it was “an empty phrase” and it would be up to member states to define the substance.
Any new trading and cooperation relationship with a foreign country would need to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states.

There is a lot of common ground: both sides want to deepen cooperation on AI, energy security, critical raw materials, quantum computing and work together in the Arctic – Carney noted that Canada shared an Arctic border with Denmark, referring to the maritime border with Greenland.

But difficulties went unspoken. While Carney described the 2016 EU-Canada comprehensive economic and trade agreement as “one of the world’s most successful trade agreements”, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify it, including France, Italy and Poland. With all three countries heading into an election year, that looks unlikely to change.

While both sides extol the virtues of deeper trade between allies, they are also pursuing policies that appear to contradict that goal. Last year Canada introduced a buy Canadian policy, to ensure Canadian suppliers get priority in public contracts. The EU is debating its own buy European law, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, now being debated in the EU, would oblige member states to meet “made in Europe” content requirements when spending public money on green technologies and electric cars.

Associate membership also raises questions about integration into the EU’s tightly guarded single market. Carney proposed “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. But the EU has long insisted that the four freedoms of its internal market – free movement of goods, services, labour and capital – are one package that cannot be split and require alignment with EU rules.
Now the applause has died down, there are plenty of tricky issues to work out, even for the closest of allies.

image.caption: Damage was caused to buildings and cars in Saudi ArabiaImage: SPA/AFP

blocks.text: At least five people were killed in the escalation between the Iran-backed Houthirebel group and the internationally recognized Yemeni government, supported by Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of a "cowardly" strike on Mecca, the holiest city in Islam and the site of the hajj and umrah pilgrimages, this week.
The rebel group denied the accusations.
Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed Saudi warplanes targeted three telecommunication towers in Taiz in southwestern Yemen.

According to the Almisrah TV channel, backed by the Houthis, one civilian was killed in the town of Abs in the northwest, with the channel later reporting that three children were killed by strikes carried out by Yemen's internationally recognized government.
In Saudi Arabia, one person was killed by shrapnel from a downed drone in the Mecca area, the country's civil defense agency said. Damage was also caused to buildings and vehicles.
This was the first reported death in Saudi Arabia in the current escalation between the two sides.

blocks.caption: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are fighting against the HouthisImage: AFP

blocks.text: Important strait taken over

The truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, agreed on in 2022, collapsed in July after the Iran-backed group allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace. As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.

The rebel group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes, from government hands.
The strait's importance has increased since Iran put restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz over the US and Israel's war with Tehran.
The conflict in Yemen has forced more than 100,000 people to flee their homes, according to UN figures.

articles.title: Judges: As AfD ascends, Germany must bolster justice system
articles.summary: German judges and prosecutors warn that the government needs to reform the laws covering state prosecutors to prevent "extremists in government" from abusing the legal system.

image.caption: German judges want to make sure state governments cannot abuse prosecution powers to influence criminal casesImage: Jennifer Brückner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The official association of German judges, the Deutscher Richterbund (DRB), has called on the federal government to tighten up the law to stop state governments from abusing prosecution powers to potentially influence criminal cases.

The prospect that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could take over the government in Saxony-Anhalt, which appears highly likely after the party's resounding election win in early September, has raised fears that "extremists in government" could steer "criminal investigations in one direction or another through directives," according to the DRB.

The AfD, sections of which are considered a threat to the German constitutional democratic order by domestic intelligence agencies, is set to take control of a state government for the first time ever in Saxony-Anhalt. This has sparked concern in the judicial system that the party could, for instance, push prosecutors away from pursuing cases against right-wing extremists.

"The top priority now is to prevent the misuse of public prosecutors' offices in Germany for partisan political purposes," DRB executive director Sven Rebehn said in a statement emailed to DW. "Currently, the law allows state justice ministries to interfere even in individual criminal proceedings. While there is a political tradition of self-restraint when issuing directives to prosecutors, this tradition can be abandoned at any time and offers no effective protection."
New report backs ban of German far-right party
State prosecutors — not independent

In Germany, unlike in many other countries, state prosecutors, along with the police, are part of the executive branch of government. This puts them under the authority of the state or federal Interior Ministries, and subject to parliamentary oversight. This dependence is seen by many constitutional lawyers as a democratic principle, as it means that prosecutors' actions can be checked by a democratically elected body. But others see it as a problem, as it opens the possibility of political influence.

German Interior Ministries, both at the federal level and in the 16 states, have the power to issue directives to prosecutors in individual cases. For instance, if some evidence has been supplied by an intelligence agency, the Interior Ministry can issue a directive to the prosecutor to keep that fact out of a court case, as disclosing it could compromise the work of the agency.

The German domestic intelligence agency, the Verfassungsschutz, which reports to the Interior Ministry, has long been a focus of the AfD's ire, as members of the party consider it politicized. The agency is charged with keeping tabs on extremist tendencies in the country. By the same token, German Justice Ministries can make a ruling over how prosecutors interpret a certain law, or how investigations are to be pursued.

One such directive was made in 2015, when the then federal justice minister, Heiko Maas, told the federal prosecutor to withdraw a report that found that state secrets had been compromised in a particular case. Maas denied that this had been the directive, and federal prosecutor Harald Range was dismissed in the ensuing power struggle.

As things stand, there is still no way to check the ministry's directives, which some see as a problem. Berlin's state prosecutor, Margarete Koppers, also has strong opinions on this point, and sees the danger as acute: "The rule of law is at risk when its rules are politically abused," a spokesperson for Koppers told DW by email. "A look at European countries that have, at various times, been under authoritarian-populist leadership — and where the structures of the rule of law were subsequently eroded — shows that this is not an unrealistic scenario." When the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) party took over in Poland, it triggered a constitutional crisis by trying to appoint judges to the constitutional court. The government of Viktor Orban in Hungary also tried to intervene in the judicial system.
EU, Poland row over judicial committee
Another option: Make directives transparent
Both the DRB and Koppers believe that removing the ministries' right to take directives is long overdue, but others in the judicial field are not so sure.

"I can understand the fear that a sword like this in the hands of the wrong people makes the executive branch a danger," said Gül Pinar, a criminal lawyer based in Hamburg who in 2020 offered expert testimony in the Bundestag on the issue.

Pinar said reform was necessary, but mainly because ministries' directives are not documented. "The people who are affected by the criminal procedures don't know that certain actions taken by the prosecutors stem from a directive, from the government, or the federal prosecutors, or the Interior Ministry," she told DW.

If the directives were documented, Pinar said, it would be possible for lawyers to examine whether they were legally sound, or whether they overstepped their authority. "We have to insert new mechanisms to check what is happening," she said.

"But the solution is not to make the state prosecutors independent," Pinar said. Hardly anyone in the judiciary, she said, doubts that the right to issue instructions stems from the principle of democracy. But she added that there were many voices, particularly amongst judges and public prosecutors, who advocate for an independent public prosecution service.

The current federal government has not shown any inclination to change the law. In a statement to the Legal Tribune Online, the Federal Justice Ministry said that the current laws provided plenty of safeguards: Ministries are prohibited from issuing "unlawful" directives, and prosecutors from following them.
In fact, according to the ministry, keeping prosecutors in the executive branch is important, because it means that they are more accountable and subject to parliamentary oversight.
Inside the AfD
The European arrest warrant problem

The relatively unique position of Germany's state prosecutors has come up at the European level before: In 2019, the European Court of Justice warned that European arrest warrants could be compromised by political influence because German state prosecutors were not independent enough: European arrest warrants are supposed to be issued by state prosecutors, but, in Germany, only judges are allowed issue them.

Pinar said allowing state prosecutors to issue arrest warrants was "not compatible with our legal system." In fact, she said, the German system safeguards more civil freedoms. "In Germany, withdrawing someone's freedom is always under the authority of the judge," she said. "I think it would better if other countries adapted their systems to ours, so that the executive branch can decide on the freedom, but was under a judge's authority."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes
articles.summary: The US has not acknowledged carrying out February's deadly strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd.

blocks.text: "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the fact-finding mission warned in a statement on Thursday.
For their latest report to the UN Human Rights Council, the mission's three independent experts investigated two of the deadliest attacks on civilians during the conflict.

On 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities.

The fact-finding mission's experts said the school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval complex also attacked that day, but that the school was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated that it was used for military purposes.

The experts said that, based on the evidence gathered - including media reports indicating that a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles - they had reasonable grounds to believe that the strike on the school was carried out by the US.

They also concluded that the school was "the intended point of impact and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage" from the attack on the IRGC complex, citing survivors as saying the school was struck twice.
The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".

Also on 28 February, Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in the town of Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities.
Again, the fact-finding mission's experts said the sports complex was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated it was used for military purposes.

They concluded by saying there were reasonable grounds to believe that the strike was carried out by the US, citing evidence including the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses PrSM missiles.
The US military has said it carried no strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon used as a PrSM.

In both incidents, the fact-finding mission's experts said there were "reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects".
The fact-finding mission's report also covers the Iranian authorities' violent repression of the mass protests that took place across Iran in December 2025 and January 2026.
The experts said it was an unprecedented escalation from past crackdowns, marked by the widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings and injuries, and extensive arrests.
They cited witnesses, health workers and victims' families as saying that security personnel positioned themselves on rooftops and other elevated positions, firing their assault rifles into crowds.
Protesters also sustained severe wounds to the head, chest and eyes from metal shotgun pellets, causing permanent blindness.

As the crackdown escalated, security forces attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded demonstrators and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care, according to the experts.
They also found that the tens of thousands of people detained during the protests faced torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal counsel.

The experts warned that the government had since intensified its use of the death penalty against protesters, with at least 29 men executed following expedited trials on charges connected to the unrest.

The fact-finding mission's report noted that it was not possible to independently verify the death toll from the crackdown, but said there were strong grounds to believe that it was significantly higher than the official figure of 3,000, the majority of whom the government identified as members of the security forces or bystanders.
The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) has said it has confirmed the killing of more than 7,000 people, almost all of them protesters.

The fact-finding mission's experts concluded that Iranian authorities had committed "many gross human rights violations" during the crackdown, and that these amounted to "the crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment and other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, and other inhumane acts, committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against a civilian population".
Iranian authorities accused the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest and blamed the deaths on what they described as "terrorists" and "rioters".

articles.summary: A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to visit the White House.

image.caption: Tamara Lich, one of the organizers of the 2022 convoy protest in Ottawa, leaves the courthouse for a lunch break in Ottawa on Thursday, April 3, 2025. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Ottawa·Breaking
A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to visit the White House.
Lich serving sentence for role in 2022 convoy protest
A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to the White House.
Lich was found guilty in April 2025 of mischief and other offences for her role in organizing and sustaining the 2022 convoy protest that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for nearly a month.
She was handed a conditional sentence last October that included 12 months under house arrest.

A month after being sentenced, Lich asked for and received permission to leave her home in Medicine Hat, Alta., to attend her grandchildren’s school. Since then, she has travelled to other provinces for her job with Rebel News.
In July, Lich asked for permission to travel internationally.

She didn't offer the court a detailed itinerary, but her request mentions attending press events at the White House, going on a seven-day Caribbean cruise with Rebel News, and travelling to Arizona to speak with Rob Schneider, a right-wing comedian whose controversial content prompted his removal from a Saskatchewan stage in 2024.

Crown prosecutors said the additional exemptions would give her a "blank cheque" to travel internationally. They opposed the request, arguing that granting it was unnecessary and would diminish the impact of her sentence "to an unacceptable extent."
Her defence said in July she had "abided by the terms of her conditional sentence to the letter."

In Justice Heather Perkins McVey's ruling Thursday, she said there was not enough evidence to show Lich's request is needed, including to maintain employment, and it would go against the principle of her sentence.
More to come.

articles.title: As global crises grow, Germany cuts development aid
articles.summary: The budget of Germany's Economic Cooperation and Development Ministry is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year. Aid organizations warn that the cuts will have severe consequences for millions…

image.caption: NGOs took to the street outside the chancellery to demonstrate against cutting development aidImage: Giulia Saudelli/DW

blocks.text: German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan opened her speech in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, with a litany of catastrophes and suffering: floods in Nepal, heat waves, forests engulfed in flames, rivers running dry, and crop failures caused by drought.

"Millions of people are facing hunger," said Radovan, of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "And one thing is clear: The climate crisis is threatening the entire world. No country can tackle it alone."

Radovan opened the debate on the federal government's proposed 2027 budget for her ministry with a stark assessment. The budget is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year, falling from just over €10 billion to just under €9.5 billion ($10.9 billion). In 2022, it stood at nearly €14 billion, meaning that the ministry's budget has been reduced by roughly one-third over the past half decade.
Fighting to end suffering in Africa's conflict zones

How does this sharp decline square with the dramatic picture painted by Germany's development minister? She pointed to a strategy she unveiled in January, when she declared that "development policy will become an even more important pillar of German security, alongside diplomacy and defense."
Funding for humanitarian aid stagnates

Aid organizations reacted skeptically to this policy shift when it was first announced, and their concerns have deepened in light of the latest funding cuts. "The renewed reductions in funding for international cooperation are further exacerbating an already critical situation," said Michael Herbst of VENRO, the umbrella organization representing around 150 development and humanitarian NGOs.

Herbst criticized the stagnant budget for humanitarian aid administered by the German Foreign Office. While it exceeded €3 billion in 2022, it has remained at just €1 billion since 2025. In light of worsening global crises, VENRO is calling for a change of course. "Next year, we will need to invest more in combating hunger because the conflict involving Iran and the dry summer are expected to trigger a sharp decline in agricultural yields," Herbst said, explaining the organization's demand for substantially higher funding.
Ten million people left without assistance

The impact of the cuts is already clearly visible, according to VENRO. A survey of its member organizations found that the number of funded projects is declining significantly. "Our sample of 34 organizations shows that, among these organizations alone, more than ten million fewer people are being reached with assistance."

"And many local partner organizations, which are indispensable to effective development cooperation and humanitarian assistance, are no longer able to operate," Herbst said. He added that the full impact of these far-reaching cuts is unlikely to become apparent for another three to four years.
A 'debt brake' exemption for development?

The federal government's belt-tightening across virtually all ministries is a consequence of the Zeitenwende announced by 2022 Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Since then, Germany has embarked on a major military buildup, increasing its defense budget year after year, while nearly all other ministries have had to make do with significantly less funding.

Herbst, a member of VENRO's executive board, is calling on the Bundestag to exempt both development cooperation and humanitarian assistance from Germany's "debt brake." "After all, exceptions have already been made for the modernization of the Bundeswehr and for military aid to Ukraine," he said. Herbst said an exemption would enable Germany to once again assume greater responsibility on the international stage.
Germany's Radovan warns SDGs unlikely to be met by 2030
Less money, less impact?

Jamila Schäfer, a member of parliament from the opposition Green Party, made a similar argument during the Bundestag debate on the Development Ministry's budget. Climate action and development cooperation, she argued, are not acts of charity but are firmly in Germany's own interest.

"Germany must invest in its defense capabilities, but security is not created through investments in the defense budget alone," Schäfer said. "Those who strengthen military security while cutting support for international stability have a blind spot in their security policy."

Nicolas Zippelius, a lawmaker from the governing center-right conservative alliance, the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), sees the ongoing cuts to development spending differently. In his view, every ministry must contribute to consolidating the federal budget. "Less money does not necessarily mean a smaller impact. Instead, it should encourage us to focus more clearly on priorities and critically review existing structures."

Zippelius dismisses demands to exempt the Development Ministry from Germany's debt brake. "The key question is whether every euro spent is directed to where it can make the greatest difference." The Christian Democrat argues that success in development cooperation, as in other areas of policy, should be judged not by the size of the budget but by the impact it achieves.
German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan in Kenya
The case for more prevention

Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, who heads the humanitarian and development aid organizationAction Against Hunger, has a very different view. "The cuts planned for the 2027 budget are short-sighted and dangerous. As a result, up to 22.6 million people worldwide could die by 2030," he said in a written statement to DW.

Cuts to development cooperation and humanitarian aid are also fiscally short-sighted, Friedrich-Rust said. "Hunger, crises and instability generate long-term costs that far exceed the cost of prevention. Those who cut spending today are merely postponing the bill and ultimately making it much more expensive," he warned.

To underscore its concerns, the Action Against Hunger alliance delivered a petition to the leaders of the governing coalition of SPD and CDU/CSU parliamentary groups on the eve of the Bundestag's budget debate. About 100,000 people added their names to the appeal, titled "Don't Balance the Budget at the Expense of Solidarity: Strengthen International Aid!"
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Manitoba adopts permanent daylight time
articles.summary: Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks.

image.caption: Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan. (Elise Amendola/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks.
Next scheduled time change was to take place Nov. 1
Daylight time will be in place permanently, Premier Wab Kinew announced in a news release Thursday.
This change means clocks will not revert to standard time on Nov. 1.
Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Just six months ago, Kinew said his government was too busy with more important matters to consider changes to the clocks.
He was asked about it in early March, shortly after B.C. announced it intended to remain on daylight time permanently.

items: Days of time change 'pretty much at the end' in Manitoba, premier suggests
Time for a survey: Province asks public to weigh in on future of time change in Manitoba

blocks.text: He later softened his stance, suggesting it may be time to revisit the issue.

Then in May, the province launched a survey, asking the public to weigh in the issue. For those who did want to see the twice-annual changes halted, the survey asked if they preferred to stay on standard or daylight time.

In its news release at the time the survey launched, the province included a link to an analysis by Manitoba Health, which concluded that eliminating the time change would be better for population health.

On Thursday, the province said nearly 72,000 votes were submitted in its survey and 92 per cent of respondents wanted to see an end to seasonal time changes, with 58 per cent preferring permanent daylight time and 34 per cent siding with standard time.

Permanent daylight time is good for health, business and families with young kids, whose routines, especially sleep cycles, can be disrupted for days with those one-hour time changes, Kinew said in the news release on Thursday.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: Australian athlete apologizes for racing with diarrhea, forfeits the Beijing competition she won
articles.summary: Australian Joanna Wietrzyk, who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition, has apologized for continuing to race and forfeited her win.

image.caption: Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia takes part in the Hyrox Beijing 2026 competition at the National Speed Skating Oval on Saturday in Beijing. She issued an apology on Thursday for continuing to race with diarrhea. (Fred Lee/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
Australian Joanna Wietrzyk, who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition, has apologized for continuing to race and forfeited her win.
Hyrox updates its competition rules after Joanna Wietrzyk left feces on shared equipment
The Hyrox athlete who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition has apologized for continuing to race, and forfeited her win.

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," Australian Joanna Wietrzyk wrote in a statement posted to Instagram Thursday morning.
"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice."

Wietrzyk explained she felt "completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness." She added that, "on reflection," she decided to retroactively forfeit her win and the points she earned.
"I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."

The graphic images of world record holder Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.

Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23.

"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then later deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.
Hyrox refunding affected participants

As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.

On Wednesday, Hyrox China announced it was refunding the entry costs to more than 1,000 participants affected by the incident, according to the South China Morning Post. A spectator at the event told the outlet that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.
Other athletes who competed in the same race described having to use equipment smeared with feces.

items: Hyrox athlete won competition while leaking diarrhea. Was she right to push through?
'Extreme' workouts drive spike in 'rhabdo' cases among young N.L. women, says doctor

blocks.text: On Monday, Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement that the organization has since changed its rules to prevent similar situations from happening again.

Its official rulebook already lists penalties for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited. Until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.

"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away," Wietrzyk wrote in her apology.
She added that she will be taking some time to "recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Verified video shows wreckage of Saudi fighter jet shot down over Yemen
articles.summary: BBC Verify tracks down the location of a Houthi video showing the wreckage of an F-15 they claim to have shot down.

blocks.text: In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number.
The fate of of the crew is not known.
The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile.
BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment.

Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran.
"They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said.

Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains.
"An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added.
