articles.title: Ninth woman's body found as South African police investigate string of deaths
articles.summary: South Africa police have cautioned against assuming that all the killings are linked but many women are afraid.

blocks.text: Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of a ninth woman's body in just two months, amid growing concern over a string of unexplained deaths east of Johannesburg.
The latest victim was found half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Dawn Park on Thursday morning, police said. Her identity has not yet been released.
The discovery follows the deaths of eight other women whose bodies have been found since July across Ekurhuleni, a major urban area of Johannesburg.

Several of the women were found partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings, which he said were "causing fear and uncertainty in our communities".

Among the victims was 38-year-old Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo, who disappeared last week after leaving her home for an afternoon run. Her body was found three days later behind a hotel in Kempton Park.

Two other victims have since been identified as Itumeleng Kekana, who had been missing since July, and 38-year-old Dineo Evelyn Motapane, whose body was discovered by the roadside in KwaThema on Tuesday.

The first of the nine bodies was discovered in Kempton Park on 15 July. A suspect was arrested two days later in connection with that case and remains in custody, but police have not linked that suspect to the other deaths.
Further bodies were discovered in August and September, including in Kempton Park, Olifantsfontein, Clayville and KwaThema.
The latest body is of a woman believed to be in her 30s and appeared to have bruises and stab wounds, local media reported.

Police have assembled a multidisciplinary team of detectives, intelligence officers, forensic experts and other specialists to investigate the deaths and establish whether there are links between the cases.
They are also pursuing a person of interest, although they have not disclosed which case or cases that person may be connected to.
"Let's not get emotional, the gloves are off," said Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi on Thursday, adding that the authorities had the capacity to deal with the killings.

Authorities have offered a 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) reward for information that could lead to arrests and have appealed to families with missing relatives to help identify the remaining victims.

The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concern about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has cautioned against speculation, saying investigators were dealing with what appeared, at this stage, to be "quite distinct, separate events".

articles.title: Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
articles.summary: Time and again, residents tracing the history of their homes discover the lives of Jewish predecessors who fled or were deported amid stories of suffering and loss.

image.caption: A 1930 photograph of Salomo Birnbaum (standing) and his family, who had to leave their home in Germany and flee to London Image: David Birnbaum/Nathan & Solomon Birnbaum Archives, Toronto

blocks.text: Over the years, many people have passed through this fourth-floor apartment in an old Berlin building. Here, at Rosenheimer Straße 40, they have sat on the sofa and gathered around the kitchen table. They have looked out the window and let their minds wander.

Marie Rolshoven has lived here with her family since 2007. "The feeling of crossing that threshold, the same one the former residents crossed for the last time, stays with you," she says. She knows that Jews once lived here, and none of them survived the Nazi era.
Driven from their homes

After the National Socialists seized power in January 1933, it quickly became clear that Jews were considered second-class citizens under Nazi rule. Even the right to remain in their homes could no longer be taken for granted.

"A racially conscious fellow citizen cannot be expected to share a household with a Jew," the Nazi party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter wrote on September 18, 1938, claiming that landlords were therefore entitled to terminate leases without notice. On April 30, 1939, the law took effect. Jewish tenants and property owners were forced to leave their homes and move into buildings designated by the authorities, referred to in Nazi jargon as "Judenhäuser"(Jewish houses).

Several people were forcibly housed in Henny and Carl Möller's apartment at Rosenheimer Straße 40. In the end, there were nine of them. In the fall of 1941, Nazi authorities began systematically deporting Jews to ghettos and camps in Eastern Europe.

blocks.caption: Jews were deported not only from Germany, but from throughout EuropeImage: Scherl/SZ Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels wrote in his diary: "The main thing is that the capital of the Reich be cleansed of Jews; and I will neither rest nor relent until this goal is fully achieved." The residents of Rosenheimer Straße were among those who were subsequently deported.
Remembering at the original site

Marie Rolshoven aims to honor the fate of these individuals. In 2016, she, along with her late mother and a friend, founded the initiative Denk Mal Am Ort (a wordplay meaning both "Think about it at the site" and "Memorial at the Site") inspired by the Amsterdam project Open Jewish Homes.

blocks.caption: Marie Rolshoven (left) hosted the niece of a Jewish woman (right) who once lived in her apartment and was murdered by the NazisImage: KUBIN e.V.

blocks.text: The idea is to invite people to the very location where everyday life once occurred. "You feel a strong connection to these individuals through the actual site," says Rolshoven. "It's different from visiting a memorial."
'My brother's bed used to be right here'
Two floors below, her neighbors had a similar experience. Denk Mal Am Ort found out that the Jewish Katzenellenbogen family had previously rented the apartment.

The family escaped Nazi Germany in 1939, just in time. "In 2018, 92-year-old Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen was invited back here, accompanied by his daughter, son-in-law, and grandson,” Rolshoven tells DW.

The Denk Mal Am Ort initiative discovered him through Facebook. Rolshoven recounts how touched the visitors were when the former resident walked in and remarked, "Yes, I remember it clearly. My brother's bed used to be right here. He was 10 when we had to leave the country."

blocks.caption: In 2018, Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen (seated middle) visited the apartment where he'd spent his childhood Image: KUBIN e.V.

blocks.text: Soon there will be no eyewitnesses left

Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen has since passed away, along with many other eyewitnesses. This highlights the importance of intergenerational remembrance, according to Rolshoven. She has already welcomed a descendant of a former resident into her home.

Claudia Samter's mother managed to escape from Berlin to Argentina, but her aunt was not as fortunate. Seeking assistance in tracing her family's history, Claudia contacted Denk Mal Am Ort. It turned out that her aunt had once been housed in Rolshoven's apartment.

Claudia Samter has already visited twice. "After all, there's no grave in a cemetery for her to visit," says Rolshoven. "We sat at the kitchen table to talk about life today and tomorrow, and we laughed a lot and cried, too. It felt good to give this space a new purpose once again."

blocks.caption: Claudia Samter (standing right) tells 'Denk Mal Am Ort' visitors about her murdered aunt, who once lived in this apartmentImage: KUBIN e.V.

blocks.text: Denk Mal Am Ort has so far organized 90 commemorative events in eight cities this year. Many young descendants attended, according to Rolshoven. "Knowing that they had stood in this stairwell and touched the same doorknob helped them."
Seeking traces of ancestors

19-year-old Adam Ethan Klein from Switzerland also wanted to learn more about his ancestors' history. "I always knew there was a story of escape, but it was never a significant topic at home,” he says.
"They'd say, ‘Yes, your great-grandparents left Germany in 1938, just in time. Luckily, otherwise you wouldn't be here today'."

Klein says his decision to dig deeper was prompted by the spread ofantisemitism, as well as the widespread slogan "Never again is now." (Editor's note: This slogan serves as a call to actively confront antisemitism, hatred, and threats to democracy today.)

The whole family was aware of a suitcase belonging to his maternal great-grandfather in the attic. However, no one ever looked inside until Adam finally opened the suitcase and discovered dozens of documents. He also found a letter from the Hanover District Court dated June 12, 1933, addressed to his great-grandfather, attorney Max Haas.

blocks.caption: This suitcase in his grandmother's attic piqued Adam's curiosityImage: privat

blocks.text: The letter stated: "As of today, following the decree issued by the Minister of Justice, you have been removed from the list of licensed attorneys."
'They were above all one thing: Jews'

Klein was profoundly affected by the letter: "With this single sentence, it became unmistakably clear to the families that they were not quite what they had aspired to be for generations: an average German family. From that moment on, they were above all one thing: Jews."

For Klein, this was a troubling realization. So was the news that someone had stabbed an ultra-Orthodox Jew to death in Zurich while shouting antisemitic slogans. The attack occurred not far from the synagogue where he had shortly before celebrated a cousin's bar mitzvah. (Editor's note: In Judaism, a bar mitzvah is a ceremony that marks a young person's coming of age in religious matters.)

"For the first time in my life, I felt that unsettling sensation of not quite belonging. Yet Zurich is my home, the city where I've lived carefree as a Jewish Swiss from birth," Adam would later write.
"That was definitely new, uncharted territory for me. I had always thought that such things don't happen in Switzerland. Maybe that was a bit naive of me," he admits.

The subject would not let him go. Adam continued his research, determined to write his high school graduation thesis about his relatives. In the spring of 2024, he set off with his parents, sister, grandmother, uncles, aunts and several cousins to visit the places where their ancestors had lived.
A magical encounter

At some point during their journey, they found themselves in Stuttgart, standing in front of a five-story building at Hölderlinstraße 55, when a man on a bike emerged from the courtyard and approached them.

"So, are you taking a guided tour of the city, or are you planning to move here?" he asked jokingly. The man was Thomas Koch, who had spent time researching the former residents of his house. When he heard the answer, "No, we're just checking out where our ancestors lived," he was thrilled.

blocks.caption: Adam Ethan Klein (right, light pants, blue sweater) and his relatives meet Thomas Koch (center, in reflector vest)Image: privat

blocks.text: Koch had already discovered that the former owners of the house, the Merzbacher brothers, sold it in 1936 for 75,000 Reichsmarks. From that amount, they had to pay 70,000 Reichsmarks in wealth taxes and the Reich Emigration Tax. The remaining sum was just enough to cover the ship fares to Brazil and the United States.

From 1937 to 1938, a family named Hirschheimer, who worked in the plywood trade, lived on the ground floor before they were forcibly relocated to a "Judenhaus." Their trail went cold in 1939, as Koch found no further records. So, he asked, "Are you the Hirschheimer family?" They were indeed.
Koch describes the encounter as magical. Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer were Adam's great-great-grandparents, and their daughter, Ilse, was married to Max Haas.
Adam Klein and Thomas Koch have kept in touch since then. The next time Adam visited Stuttgart, he was invited over for coffee and cake.

blocks.caption: Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer lived with their daughter Ilse in the place where Thomas Koch now livesImage: privat

blocks.text: Adam was impressed by the beautiful apartment. "It was fascinating to imagine how my ancestors once lived there, and it probably wasn't that different. Back then, there was likely coffee and cake as well."
Adam showed Koch photos of his grandmother, Ilse, who had married at the synagogue in Stuttgart, standing in the living room in her wedding gown. "In front of the door that we still have," says Koch.

“It was really moving to discover new roommates in a historical context set in the past. And I think this experience — this process of putting myself in their shoes — is a deeply empathetic one that simply brings us together through this apartment.”
Shattered identities

Ilse and Max Haas found refuge in England, while the Hirschheimers emigrated to Switzerland in 1939. Adolf Hirschheimer died in 1940 from a heart condition, but Adam, his great-great-grandson, believes he "certainly also died of a broken heart."

blocks.caption: Thomas Koch (right) and Adam Ethan Klein have presented their joint investigation to audiences on several occasionsImage: privat

blocks.text: Auguste was brought to England by her son-in-law, Max, where the family felt homesick. "There, we were the Jews; here, we are the Germans. Try figuring that out," Ilse Haas wrote to a friend. Adam chose these lines as the title for his thesis.
Adam's great-grandparents could not find peace after being stripped of their homeland. From England, they eventually went to Israel and, at some point, returned to Europe — to Switzerland.

"At the end of their lives, my great-grandparents settled just a two-hour drive from their old homeland," Adam wrote. "When I look at their lives through the eyes of a great-grandson, it becomes clear that after breaking ties with Germany, they never managed to put down roots anywhere again."

"Remembering is important because, ultimately, we have to learn from history," says Adam. "And I think every single person has a responsibility— and the power — to actively keep memories alive. And hopefully, that can happen even without eyewitnesses.” For example, in his ancestors' former apartment.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds
articles.summary:
Fact-finding mission says military strikes on school and sports facility in ⁠February constitute war ⁠crimes

A UN fact-finding mission on Iran has said there are reasonable grounds to…

blocks.text: A UN fact-finding mission on Iran has said there are reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in ⁠February, and that these constituted war ⁠crimes.
It also found Iranian ​authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.

The findings by the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN human rights council in Geneva, examined the ⁠US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that begun in late December.
US officials have previously said military ⁠operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.

The UN experts said they found ​reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the ‌Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in the city of ‌Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
It constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to ‌civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.

blocks.caption: A rubble-strewn classroom at Shajareh Tayyebeh school. Photograph: Vahid Salemi/AP

blocks.text: According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.

“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”

In June the US president, Donald Trump, said ‌that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were probably responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated ​the inquiry but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes.

The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that ⁠US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.

The UN mission found ​that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic ​attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late ​December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.

Rights groups say bystanders were among ​those killed during the biggest crackdown ‌since Shia Muslim clerics took ​power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists ​and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the US and Israel.

The investigation said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was probably far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.

The government’s response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

articles.title: Jürgen Klopp's first Germany squad includes 44 players
articles.summary: Germany's new head coach Jürgen Klopp has named a huge squad for his first four games, splitting them into two groups. A host of new faces is included.

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp announced an XXL squad for his first games in chargeImage: John Macdougall/AFP

blocks.text: Jürgen Klopp's Germany era has begun as the new head coach announced his first squad on Thursday.

To manage the newly organized international break that sees the September and October pauses merged into one, Klopp selected 44 players splitting them into two squads across the four games. Klopp did add though, that Nico Schlotterbeck, Jamal Musiala and Serge Gnabry might stay for the whole two weeks. Goalkeeper Finn Dahmen is also in both squads as Klopp wants to take a closer look at him.
"It's unusual to have four games in two weeks," said Klopp at the press conference.
"I want to get to know as many players as possible. There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.
"There are few names here that will surprise, but we wanted it to be a part of their development," he added.
"We didn't look at what we were missing but rather what we have and realized how much football talent we have."

There were a total of 11 new players included, with the biggest surprise being Hoffenheim's Bambase Conte, Stuttgart defender Finn Jeltsch, Celtic's Mika Baur, and Freiburg's Derry Scherhant. Younes Ebnoutalib (23), Frankfurt's breakout forward was included, with Klopp saying he was a "huge talent" who was "hugely delighted" to be included.

Felix Keidel, the 23-year-old midfielder from Elversberg who has played just three Bundesliga games was another big surprise. Keidel can also play at right back, but has been predominately used as a holding midfielder since the small-town team won promotion to the top flight.
Oliver Baumann, Deniz Undav and Leroy Sane were not included.
Politically, Klopp wants to win back the flag

Klopp spoke at length on many subjects, saying he wanted more from his players, that how the team played was more important than who played, and that his whole career had prepared him for this job. He also spoke on what it means to be German in the modern political and social climate.

"I hope that I don't have to talk about politics in future press conferences but from my sporting perspective, I would like to win back the flag. I don't want national pride to be left to the wrong people. I am so proud to do this job and we are a wonderful country," Klopp said.

"It, this team and sport, is here to make us feel better and to develop a sense of togetherness and feel the power of sport," he said, citing Zverev's recent success in tennis and the basketball World Cup. "We are responsible for creating this atmosphere."
ter Stegen one of many old faces who return to Germany squad

Marc-Andre ter Stegen returns to the Germany squad after a lengthy injury layoff, and Klopp called him the number one at the moment. The 33-year-old goalkeeper, who is now playing his club football at Ajax, last appeared for Germany in the Nations League Finals last summer.
"I've known Marc-Andre for a long time," Klopp said.
"He has the right amount of experience. He is a keeper that can play with the ball and he is also an excellent shot-stopper. Everything depends on performance."

Said El Mala was included. The Cologne youngster was a surprise inclusion in Germany's World Cup qualifying campaign in November 2025, but didn't make an appearance. He is widely expected to be one of the faces of this new Germany team under Klopp.
Notable absences in this first Germany squad under the new boss were Deniz Undav, Leroy Sane and Oliver Baumann.

Germany's international break starts in Amsterdam against the Netherlands on September 24, before a home game in Augsburg against Greece three days later. On October 1, Germany are to play Serbia in Munich before traveling to Thessaloniki to play Greece in the final game of the international break on October 4.

articles.title: EU announces plan to restrict social media access for children
articles.summary: Under the plans, only children over 15 would be able to set up their own social media accounts.

blocks.text: The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-16s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.
Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.
Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.

The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove their platforms were safe by design, while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat".
She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".
Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.
Von der Leyen has previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe, saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".
The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address to the EU Parliament on Wednesday.
Some individual EU countries have already announced their own separate plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.

articles.title: Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
articles.summary: Mustafa Suleyman says he believes rival AI firm Anthropic is in effect teaching Claude it "may be conscious".

blocks.text: Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets.
That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us".

Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week, external, in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people".

In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.
He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human.
"AIs are not conscious," he wrote.
"They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.
"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."
The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry.
Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity.
Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

"I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said.
"Everybody must be aligned."
Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.

Suleyman's comments reflects Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external, a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence".
This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control".
The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve.
Additional reporting by Henry Moore

articles.title: Frank Stronach faces sentencing hearing on indecent assault conviction
articles.summary: When his judge-alone trial began in February, Frank Stronach was facing 12 charges related to allegations of sexual assault from seven women. In a sentencing hearing Thursday, the 94-year-old…

image.caption: Earlier this year, Canadian billionaire Frank Stronach was facing 12 charges related to allegations of sexual assault from seven women dating back almost 50 years. A number of those charges were withdrawn. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

When his judge-alone trial began in February, Frank Stronach was facing 12 charges related to allegations of sexual assault from seven women. In a sentencing hearing Thursday, the 94-year-old businessman could be sentenced on just one of those charges — indecent assault.
Businessman initially faced 12 charges, still faces 2nd trial in Newmarket next year
WARNING: This story refers to sexual assault allegations and may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

When his judge-alone trial began in a Toronto courtroom in February, Canadian billionaire Frank Stronach was facing 12 charges related to allegations of sexual assault from seven women dating back almost 50 years.
But in a sentencing hearing Thursday, the 94-year-old founder of auto-parts giant Magna International could be sentenced on just one of those charges — indecent assault.

On the indecent assault charge, one of the women had told the court that Stronach invited her to a midtown Toronto apartment sometime in the fall of 1977 and, while there, bent her over the arm of a chair, lifted up her skirt and tried to rape her.
Stronach had been charged with attempted rape and indecent assault for that particular incident. But during the course of the trial, the Crown dropped the attempted rape charge.

In her decision, Ontario Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy agreed that much of what the witness described had happened, but also agreed with the Crown's decision to withdraw the attempted rape charge because it was unclear whether Stronach would have been able to penetrate the woman based on her state of dress at the time.

Still, Molloy referred to it as "gross and disgusting conduct," which is why she found him guilty of indecent assault. The offence is a historical charge, having been repealed from the Criminal Code in 1983. That means anyone charged similarly today would face a sexual assault charge.

In June, Molloy also found Stronach guilty of sexual assault related to another woman who said Stronach groped her in his Toronto Harbourfront condo sometime in 1983 or 1984. The woman said she had gone to meet him for dinner to discuss why she had been fired as a waitress at his then restaurant, Rooney's. She said Stronach invited her to his condo, which is where he groped her.

Molloy said she was "completely convinced" by the woman's evidence. Molloy did, however, "with considerable trepidation," describe it as a minor sexual assault, saying that the conduct was at the "low end" of the spectrum of sexual assault.
2nd conviction granted mistrial

However, weeks after the decision, emails were presented in court from the woman's lawyer in a separate civil complaint. Stronach's lawyer Leora Shemesh alleged those emails told a story inconsistent with the woman's testimony in the criminal trial.
Molloy then granted a mistrial on the sexual assault conviction. The Crown is appealing that decision.

Throughout the trial, which lasted more than two months, the Crown withdrew a number of charges following the testimony and cross-examination of some of the complainants, saying there was not sufficient evidence to sustain findings of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on those particular counts.
By the time Molloy was set to render her decision in June, Stronach was facing five counts related to three women.

items: Crown appealing post-verdict mistrial in Frank Stronach sexual assault conviction
Canadian businessman Frank Stronach found guilty of sexual assault, indecent assault

blocks.text: All of the initial seven complainants, whose allegations span the period between 1977 and 1990, testified in court, offering an emotional account of the sexual offences they say they experienced at the hands of Stronach.
Stronach, who was in court every day but never took the witness box in his own defence, had denied the allegations and pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Meanwhile, Stronach is set to face another trial in Newmarket, Ont., next year. When Stronach was initially arrested in June 2024, he was charged with 18 offences involving 13 complainants. But the case was split into two trials later that year.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Mark Gollom is a Toronto-based reporter with CBC News. He covers Canadian and U.S. politics and current affairs.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: 'Blood is on our hands': Haitian honour student's death sparks outcry over ICE ankle monitors
articles.summary: Pierre Damas Bel fled Haiti and came to the U.S. with a dream of becoming a neurosurgeon. But after U.S. immigration authorities fitted the 20-year-old university student with an ankle monitor, he…

image.caption: A proud member of the Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps at Springfield High School, Pierre Damas Bel was an aspiring doctor and neuroscience student at Wright State University. After U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement fitted him with an ankle monitor in July, he walked into highway traff

blocks.text: Haitian student in Ohio ended his life over 'humiliating' ICE ankle monitor, family believes
Warning: This story contains descriptions of suicide.
Decorated with academic and athletic awards, Pierre Damas Bel was well on his way to fulfilling his dream of becoming a neurosurgeon.

Described by teachers as a "student of the highest calibre" and a "deeply dedicated" member of his community, Bel was an honour student, captain of the varsity soccer team and volunteer at a food bank in Springfield, Ohio.
But this summer, Bel lost the protected immigration status that allowed him to legally live in the U.S. after fleeing the ongoing instability in Haiti in 2024.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) fitted the 20-year-old Wright State University student with an ankle monitor in late July as an "alternative to detention." But the device prevented him from playing soccer, and he reportedly began to be bullied by classmates and felt he was "treated like an animal."
"I came here to study, to build my future … not to be treated like [a] criminal," he wrote in a post.

Bel was one of about 350,000 Haitians living and working in the U.S. who lost temporary protected status (TPS) after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowed the Trump administration to revoke the humanitarian protection.
Homeland Security's deportation campaign began immediately.
"Those with terminated TPS are in our nation illegally," it posted alongside a video showing Haitian migrants in chains, escorted onto a repatriation flight on Aug. 27.

Once a lieutenant in his high school's Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps (JROTC) program and described as a "natural leader" who would become a "great American," Bel was the only one in the Wright State ROTC program not to be given a uniform because of the monitor, his father says.
The following Monday, Bel walked into traffic on a nearby highway and was struck by a semi-truck, according to Ohio State Highway Patrol.
He died on the scene. His family believes it was a suicide.
'100% preventable'
In the following days, memorials were held in his honour in Ohio and across the U.S., including New York City. Many held ICE's immigration crackdown responsible for his death.
"Racist anti-Haitian campaign murdered Pierre Damas Bel," one woman's sign in New York read.
Asked to respond to advocates' allegations that the shame of the ankle monitor drove Bel to suicide, ICE told CBC any attempts to blame the agency for his death are false.
"No one is required to stay in the United States illegally and wear a GPS monitor," the agency wrote, adding that self-deportation is an option.
But Yola Lamarre, a friend of Bel, says ICE's response oversimplifies Bel's mental health crisis and blames the young man for his own death.
"We have to be honest in where blood is on our hands," she told CBC News.
Lamarre, who saw Bel as a little brother, said his death was "100 per cent preventable" if he had been treated more humanely.
"He told me how he would try to wear a certain wardrobe to hide the ankle monitor," she said.
"He just wanted belonging. He just wanted acceptance."

items: At least 47 people killed in violent weekend attacks in Haiti, UN says
Who can protect Haiti? An inside look at a country trying to repel violent gangs

blocks.text: Haitians were granted TPS after the 2010 earthquake that killed more than 300,000 people in the Caribbean country. Other crises, including cholera outbreaks, Hurricane Sandy and the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, prompted further extensions.

After failed attempts to end Haiti's TPS in Trump's first term, the Department of Homeland Security announced in June 2025 it was ending it, saying the situation had "improved enough that it is safe for Haitian citizens to return home." Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department tells its citizens not to travel to Haiti due to the risk of "crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care."

The ankle monitoring program Bel was subjected to appears to be part of a larger strategy by ICE to "make life so miserable" that Haitians will self-deport, said Carl Ruby, senior pastor at Central Christian Church in Springfield, Ohio, a city where at least 10,000 of its roughly 60,000 residents are Haitian.
"They're afraid to go outside of their homes," said Ruby, whose church saw its Haitian attendance plummet from about 50 people to two.
Residents 'shackled'
Ruby said hundreds of Springfield residents — including teenagers, elderly and pregnant people — have been "shackled" with ankle monitors, often leading to deep shame and social isolation.
"Their old friends start to pull back from them because they're afraid that if they're with a person who has an ankle monitor, that they might be apprehended."
Critics like Ohio Democratic congressman Greg Landsman say the electronic monitoring program also unfairly humiliates law-abiding migrants.
"They aren't criminals," wrote Landsman. "It's all so wrong and cruel to pick on anybody, especially a group this vulnerable."
Canadian immigration 'very difficult' for Haitians in U.S., says advocate
Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, said his community members are caught in a catch-22: no longer safe in the U.S., they also have nowhere to go.
"There is no country that is willing to welcome us," said Dorsainvil, who lost TPS himself. "We cannot go to work. We live in fear and anxiety on a daily basis."
The end of TPS has had a chilling effect across the wider Haitian diaspora in the U.S.

items: Why is Trump so focused on Haiti?
Haitians in the U.S. brace for deportation as Trump ends their protected status

blocks.text: At a Springfield strip mall, once a hub of economic activity with several Haitian-owned businesses, storefronts were locked or shuttered altogether when CBC visited last week.
One store employee, who asked not to be identified because of his immigration status, described the situation as a "catastrophe."
"There are many people who don't have enough to eat, who are sick, who don't have access to medical care … and no way to get to a doctor," the asylum seeker told CBC in French.
'There's no life for them,' restauranteur says of Haitians who lost protected status
Other businesses are struggling to pay their bills.

Claucia Dossous, a Haitian American who runs T-Co Islands Restaurant in Columbus, Ohio, said ending TPS has "broken everybody's life" after Haitians who frequented her restaurant were forced out of work.
"I pay for the price, too."
Looking to Canada
The climate of fear has led some Haitians to try moving to Canada.

More Haitian nationals file for asylum at the land border than any other country so far this year, according to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA). Figures from the Immigration and Refugee Board show that more than 27,000 Haitians are awaiting decisions — about 1/10th of all pending asylum claims.
Haitian American activist Guerline Jozef wants Canada to open more humanitarian pathways for Haitians who no longer feel safe in their country.

"We find ourselves in a place where we cannot leave, we cannot stay. And the only option they are giving them is to be kidnapped and be deported to the same place that they have fled," said Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance in San Diego, Calif.
Canada returning Haitian asylum seekers to U.S. immigration authorities, says activist
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada told CBC it "cannot speculate on future policy decisions" but highlighted temporary measures for Haitian nationals in place until October.
But for those outside Canada, those measures are only available to family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents.
Ruby described the case of one family who was a part of their congregation who survived several kidnapping attempts in Haiti.
Because one of them had a sister in Canada, they were able to join her. The day they arrived in Canada, they received letters from ICE telling them their TPS was over and to self-deport.
"They got out just in time," he said. "But that option just isn't available to very many people."
Instead, Jozef said many of the people who try to flee the U.S. into Canada are turned away.

Under the Safe Third Country Agreement, refugees who first arrive in the U.S. are barred from seeking asylum in Canada, barring certain exceptions. More than 1,100 asylum seekers were returned to U.S. immigration authorities under this agreement so far this year, according to the CBSA.
Montreal migrant advocate Frantz André said the agreement now effectively allows for "deportation by proxy" when Canadian agents turn back Haitian migrants knowing they will be deported by the U.S.
"The United States is no longer a safe country for hundreds of thousands of people," he said. "People are in despair."
If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:

items: Canada's Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.

articles.title: Trump threatens EU with ‘serious tariffs’ after proposal to make Canada first associate member – Europe live
articles.summary:
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen says such a partnership is for the European Union’s ‘common strength’

US president Donald Trump has threatened the European Union…

blocks.text: Morning opening: Trump threatens Europe, again

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

US president Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with “serious tariffs” and a cut to trade after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first ever associate member, calling the idea “laughable”.

Suggesting the move was a “hostile act”, the US president told reporters he could put “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

European Commision president Ursula von der Leyen insisted yesterday that “this is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength,” and deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill repeated this line this morning in response to Trump’s overnight threats.

Canadian prime minister Mark Carney – fresh from watching Everton’s Carabao Cup win over Wolverhampton Wanderers in Liverpool – will address the European parliament late morning. Let’s see if he has anything to say on this.

blocks.caption: Mark Carney and Andy Burnham before the Carabao Cup Third Round match between Everton and Wolverhampton Wanderers at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, England. Photograph: Tony McArdle/Everton FC/Getty Images

blocks.text: Separately, our attention is increasingly turning to Germany, where embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to join the campaign trail today in Berlin ahead of this weekend’s two state elections that just could determine his political future.

blocks.caption: German chancellor Friedrich Merz attends a meeting of the German government’s cabinet in Berlin, Germany. Photograph: Filip Singer/EPA

blocks.text: Powerful German state leaders from his party have rallied behind the chancellor as speculation builds that his days in office may be numbered, and he cancelled his trip to the UN general assembly next week.

Our Berlin correspondent Deborah Cole will be joining us just after 11am to answer your questions about Merz’s future, the two state elections, and what’s next for Germany. You can post your questions to her below the line from 9am.
Lots for us to cover today.
It’s Thursday, 17 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 20m agoMorning opening: Trump threatens Europe, again

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels

The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules.

blocks.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen greeting Canada's prime minister Mark Carney during her annual keynote address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, eastern France. Photograph: Christophe Licoppe/EUROPEAN UNION/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: It remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. When the UK was negotiating its departure from the bloc and post-Brexit relationship, EU officials repeatedly said there was no status that enabled a foreign country to be half in and half out of the single market.
The phrase itself took EU insiders by surprise since von der Leyen had not used the term when she briefed senior EU diplomats ahead of her speech last Friday.

One EU diplomat said member states were “generally very supportive of ambition” in the EU-Canada relationship, but had been slightly worried in recent weeks that von der Leyen was overpromising on Canada.

“‘Associate membership’ sounds like a nice headline but in reality 10 member states have still not ratified Ceta,” the person said, referring to the EU-Canada trade agreement that was agreed 10 years ago.
A second EU diplomat described associate membership as “an empty phrase”.
Martin Leng at the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics thinktank said a world in flux was “pushing the EU towards far greater flexibility in its relations with third states”.

He said von der Leyen’s speech, with its focus on different sectoral areas of cooperation “points to the ambition and strategic breadth of the associate membership which the parties have in mind but also suggests that, in reality, Canada’s ‘membership’ may consist of ‘plugging in’ to existing programmes and frameworks, such as the European Defence Agency, rather than joining the union in any traditional sense”.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Yemen’s war continues to threaten oil supplies– but what about its people?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast raised fears for global trade and energy supplies, while more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the…

blocks.text: Good morning. The lightning advance of Houthi militants along the west coast of Yemen over the past week has prompted fears of a spiralling conflict in the region and a new oil supply crisis.

For families living in the Middle East’s poorest country, the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years is a crisis upon a catastrophe, with escalating civilian casualties and at least 100,000 displaced in recent days.

Houthi fighters have captured strategic islands across a critical Red Sea trade route, the Bab al-Mandab strait, one of the most important shipping routes in the world – almost 15% of global sea trade passes through it. The strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime, has remained largely blocked since the US and Israel launched airstrikes in February, so the prospect of Iran and its allies exerting pressure on two maritime choke points has global implications. The price of crude oil has already begun to spike.

For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, about this new and dangerous dimension to the ongoing war in Yemen, and why fears over oil and global trade must not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis. First, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Key allies of Andy Burnham have warned the prime minister not to back down over his promises to put water companies under public control, after details emerged about the prime minister’s plan to give mayors more oversight of the industry.

Environment | Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.
Health | Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found.

Europe | The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.
UK news | Police searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex border have found a body.

blocks.text: In depth: The fight for Yemen’s Red Sea coast

blocks.caption: Yemen refugees arrive in Djibouti as intensified fighting drives displacement. Photograph: International Organization for Migration/Reuters

blocks.text: The current escalation of violence in Yemen has its roots in a civil war that broke out in 2014 between the Yemeni army and the Houthi movement, which champions Yemen’s Shia Muslim minority. A year later, the Houthis – part of Iran’s “axis of resistance”, a loose coalition of armed groups that includes Hamas and Hezbollah – toppled the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Al-Muslimi grew up in a remote mountain village in Yemen, where his family made honey, one of the country’s most lucrative and popular exports. His mother used to tease him because the bees didn’t recognise him after he spent long periods studying away from home – he was the only person in his family who had to wear a beekeeping suit.

Al-Muslimi now writes about how the years-long internecine conflict has had a devastating impact on the honey trade and the farmers who tend Yemeni bees. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014, mainly through aerial bombardment by the Saudi-backed coalition that supports the Yemeni government, which has resumed this week. About 4.5 million people – the population of Birmingham and Greater Manchester combined – have already been displaced by fighting over the past decade, while the UN estimates that more than 18.2 million – twice the population of London – are in dire need of humanitarian assistance.

The situation now is “worse than 2015”, says Al-Muslimi, with global attention diverted to crises in Syria, Sudan, and Ukraine and now focused on oil prices and regional consequences. “There is even less willingness to help civilians.”

After the Houthis captured the port city of Mocha, birthplace of the global coffee trade, last week, Al-Muslimi heard local media reports of more than 240 pregnant women ready to give birth without accessible healthcare.
“It’s absolutely nuts,” he says. “This is a country that was already suffering so many things, including indifference.”
How has the conflict escalated in the past week?

It has been plain for months to Yemen-watchers that the Houthis were preparing for a significant offensive, says al-Muslimi. This erupted about a week ago with the militants seizing control of parts of the west coast and gaining a hold over the Bab al-Mandab strait, including the strategic port of Mocha and key islands of Perim, Greater and Lesser Hanish in the 20-mile stretch of water that forms a natural chokepoint on the trade route connecting Asia with Europe.

With government supporters in disarray, the degree of division among anti-Houthi forces is complicating the fight back. The Houthis have achieved what Al-Muslimi calls “the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years”.

Since then, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the bombing of a critical east-west oil pipeline. On Wednesday a military spokesperson for the Houthis denied attempting to fly a drone close to the holy city of Mecca, and claimed that Saudi Arabia has carried out as many as 450 airstrikes in Yemen ‌this week in retaliation. The ongoing aggression is driving fears that more Muslim nations could be drawn into the conflict.
What does it mean for global oil supply?

If ​the Houthis were to close the Bab al-Mandab strait, vessels would be forced to reroute all the way around the southern tip of Africa. The consequences for the global economy could be dire, particularly when taken along with the ongoing blockade of Hormuz.

With Iran and its Houthi allies controlling potentially a third of energy trade globally, “it’s more dangerous than a nuclear bomb,” says Al-Muslimi bluntly, “especially at a time when the world still depends massively on this type of energy”.

Attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which is now closed for repairs and has been crucial for moving oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will add further pressure to global supplies.

Al-Muslimi advises caution over Houthi claims that they don’t intend to impose transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab. The UN security council has seen evidence that, since the militants started attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023, in response to Israel’s decimation of Gaza, the Houthis have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage.

Meanwhile, Saudi anger with Iran for assisting Houthi attacks saw the cancellation of a meeting with Gulf states about the future of the strait of Hormuz on Monday. Reports in the early hours today that Saudi Arabia may be offering more crude cargoes through Oman saw the price of Brent crude drop to $104.59 a barrel after hitting $108 earlier this week. But for perspective, it was trading at $80 a barrel in early July.

This comes as the average price of diesel in the US hit $6 per gallon for the first time last week, with the Iran war, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, continuing to squeeze supply.
What does it mean for the region?

The UN security council held an emergency meeting in New York on Tuesday to discuss the escalating violence in Yemen and threats to maritime security, with members urging maximum restraint to avoid the situation devolving into a wider regional war. The conflict is the first test of a mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, announced in August – but Saudi has yet to publicly call on either for assistance.

Meanwhile, Al-Muslimi says the US, a close Saudi ally, faces a dilemma. The States reached a truce with the Houthis in May 2025, after conducting airstrikes against the group after attacks on Red Sea shipping. “The existing truce gives both sides reasons for restraint,” he says. “For Trump, preserving that arrangement helps keep the US away from another costly Middle Eastern military confrontation while it remains engaged in the strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have equally strong incentives to not be drawn into conflict with the US, which caused them serious damage in the 2025 bombing campaign.”

Yesterday the Guardian confirmed that officials from the US had met Houthi leaders over the weekend in Oman, where they received assurances that the ceasefire still held and that the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. While Trump condemned the Houthi advance for threatening freedom of navigation, he has far rejected any military response in support of Riyadh.

Al-Muslimi calls for a more coherent international approach to his country, which he considers one of the least understood in the region. Yemen analysts have frequently criticised the US and allies for approaching Yemen’s challenges with a focus on security rather than diplomacy or development, while internal instability has been exploited by larger regional powers to fight their own proxy battles.

Most importantly, he says: “While this new international dimension of Yemen’s war makes the country strategically more important to the world, it should not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis”.

articles.title: Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
articles.summary: There is no doubt over the outcome of this vote, but for the Kremlin they are still an important moment.

blocks.text: Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reports
BySteve Rosenberg
Russia editorReporting fromMoscow and Dmitrov
The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).
That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.
This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.
Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.
But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say.
"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.
That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?
Far from it.
For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans

blocks.text: This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans
As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.
I said no surprises. But there have been some.
"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.
The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.
"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."
In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:
"The Communist Party, onwards we go!
"We're with the people, don't you know?"
More X Factor than exit poll.

Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:
"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"
It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine

blocks.text: Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine

"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.
"In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."

I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.

But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.
And if a party doesn't support the war?

One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.

Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.
"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.
"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.

"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular

blocks.text: Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular
For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.

"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."
Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.

The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.
Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.
In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.
The war is front and centre of people's minds here.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation"

blocks.text: Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation"

"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."
"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."
Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.

"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."
Expectations are low that this election will change much.

"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.

"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

articles.title: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
articles.summary: Austin Tice’s abduction was approved by Syria’s former leader Bashar al-Assad, a source claims.

blocks.text: US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the BBC can reveal.
A member of the group which detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.

Tice was seen getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed they had stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist had been opportunistic.
But we have uncovered evidence that, in fact, his disappearance was anything but chance.

In a new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, we reveal the findings of a years-long investigation into what happened to Tice, who had been reporting on Syria's civil war at the time.
His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive US presidents.
Georgetown University law student Tice, who had served as a US Marines captain, was last seen in a video - blindfolded and in apparent distress - posted more than a month after his capture.
As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons. Tice was not one of them.
We obtained co-ordinates from an intelligence source for multiple locations US authorities suspected he could have been held at, and searched for him for more than a month, but found no sign of him.
A former Syrian commander has said Tice was executed. Others have questioned this account and no remains have been found.

But in the aftermath of the regime's collapse, we did uncover secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice - hundreds of pages of internal records providing the first definitive proof that it was the regime that had held the journalist.
Two crucial questions remained unanswered, however: how exactly had Tice been taken in the first place? And, who was responsible for his abduction?

We have spoken to a number of men from the regime involved in Tice's detention, and have reviewed recordings of discussions about it. One man we spoke to, Abu Ali, is a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia which was fiercely loyal to Assad.

He says the abduction operation began when Tice's driver - who multiple sources say had been passing the regime information for some time - told a senior NDF member that Tice was moving through rebel-held areas, reporting on the opposition.

Tice had pushed into areas most journalists deemed too dangerous and was writing front-page stories for the Washington Post. The Assad regime was cracking down on anyone highlighting its human rights abuses.

We have been told the NDF member Tice's driver spoke to was Sakr Rustom - not just any NDF militia contact, but nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, one of Assad's most trusted security figures and head of the NDF.
The information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, Abu Ali says, who is then said to have telephoned Assad.
"Bring him to us," Assad replied, claims Abu Ali.
Abu Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.
But Tice was not taken immediately. The driver, Abu Ali says, suggested that he and the NDF continue watching him, to uncover more about what he was doing.
"He trusts me," Abu Ali recalls the driver saying.
Some time later, the driver reported back that Tice's actions seemed suspicious, Abu Ali says.
Tice, as a trained marine, would sometimes share his military experience with rebel fighters - according to several people we spoke to - and would correct fighters on how they used their weapons.

To the men watching him, that behaviour made Tice look less like a journalist and more like someone from the CIA. The BBC has found no evidence to suggest this was the case, and a former senior US official responsible for part of Tice's case has denied he was an intelligence officer.

In the days before Tice vanished, the driver made one particularly brazen move while Tice was interviewing rebel fighters. He secretly took the American's backpack, containing his MacBook, a satellite transmitter and other personal items, for regime operatives to look through, multiple sources say.

On 11 August 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse on the western edge of Damascus, a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. There was a swimming pool, Free Syrian Army fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey, Tice revealed in what would become his final tweet.
"Hands down, best birthday ever," he wrote.
Then came the time for Tice to leave Syria. He had told various people he was planning to take time out in Lebanon.

But he was not heading to safety. He was heading to a state facility where Hassan had an office, in an area called Tahouneh on the outskirts of Damascus, according to several sources. Abu Ali was waiting there for Tice.
Abu Ali says Tice's driver told him that when he drew up to the gates, he pulled out a gun.

Tice laughed at first, Ali recalls the driver saying, apparently believing the man he trusted was joking. But the driver told Tice he was serious, Abu Ali says, and the journalist realised what was happening.
According to Ali, Tice pulled out his chequebook and pleaded with the driver to name his price, rather than go through with the kidnap.
NDF militia members then grabbed Tice, covering his eyes, Abu Ali says.
Another NDF member told us he would never forget Tice's expression as he realised he had been betrayed. Abu Ali says Hassan immediately called President Assad to tell him they had the American.
For years, the identity of Tice's driver has remained a mystery.
The BBC spoke to more than 20 people to discover who he was, with the trail eventually leading to the city of Homs, and the family of a man called Hamid Abu Obeid.
They confirmed he was the man who had driven Tice away, an account also supported by multiple NDF members. But by the time we identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared.
His family say they do not know where he is, and fear for his safety. They say they were not aware of Hamid's involvement in Tice's case, and learned about it from him afterwards.
But they did give a motive for his betrayal of Tice.
The Abu Obeid family, Palestinian refugees from Gaza, live in poverty. Under Syrian law they are not entitled to Syrian citizenship and live under significant restrictions.

According to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon, in return for delivering Tice - life-changing rewards. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a pistol.

Then, after Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says her husband was called by a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the US embassy, hoping it might help him secure asylum.

Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed.
Not long after he disappeared, she says masked men - some dressed in military clothes - visited and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other devices.

The wishes of Abu Obeid's wife now chillingly mirror those of Tice's mother and family. On opposite sides of a disappearance that began more than a decade ago, both families are searching for the same thing: a loved one who vanished, and an answer to where he went.

articles.title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
articles.summary:
As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild…
articles.byline: Patrick Greenfield. Photographs by Scott Creel

blocks.text: It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.

But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.

blocks.caption: Two months after they set out, the brothers and sisters met again, spending a day together before separating.  Photograph: MSU

blocks.text: From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.

The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.

Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.

“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”

The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.

Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.

Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.

But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.

“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.

blocks.caption: African wild dogs have been endangered for decades, with only 6,600 or so adults remaining of 39 populations across the continent.  Photograph: MSU

blocks.text: “If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

articles.title: Fiji declares national HIV emergency as Pacific nation grapples with surge in cases
articles.summary:
Government estimates that one in 60 adults in Fiji now living with HIV, as escalating use of methamphetamine fuels ‘epidemic’

Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency amid a spike in…

blocks.text: Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency amid a spike in infections as the Pacific nation grapples with a correlating rise in methamphetamine use.

The country’s health and medical services minister, Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu, said in a statement on social media that an outbreak-level response was no longer sufficient to address what he described an “epidemic”.
“Today I am formally declaring a national health emergency in Fiji,” he said. “This decision recognises the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent coordinated response our country now needs.”
The health minister said the government estimates that one in every 60 adults in Fiji is now living with HIV.
“Five years ago, the estimate was one in 167. In 2025, we recorded 2,060 new HIV diagnoses,” he said, adding that one in 50 pregnant women has HIV.
The emergency declaration followed on from a cabinet decision on 9 September and would require a coordinated response, he added.

Home to less than one million people, the Pacific nation is facing one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally, according to UNAIDS, which said that new infections spiked 12-fold between 2010 and 2025.

Fiji’s location as a drug-running hub coupled with the escalating use of methamphetamine locally has fuelled the rapid spread of HIV, a situation worsened by unsafe injecting and a lack of access to clean needles. Low health awareness, cultural stigma and inadequate testing and treatment have exacerbated the crisis.
Among HIV cases in Fiji with a known mode of transmission, over half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use, according to UNAIDS.
Of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in Fiji in 2025, only 39% were aware of their HIV status and only 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment, the UN said.
